# Building and running on Windows 11 (gfx1151, TheRock ROCm wheels)

First Windows build of this branch, 2026-09-02. Summary: **no source changes were
needed** - the branch compiles and runs as-is with the TheRock ROCm SDK for
Windows. MTP decode reaches parity with the Linux numbers (30.1-30.7 t/s code
vs 31.1 in BENCHMARKS.md); prefill lands at ~71% of the Linux SSD-lazy rate
(278-284 t/s at 4.4K depth vs 396). Single machine, single day of measurements -
treat everything below as n=1.

## Test machine

| | |
|---|---|
| System | AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 (Strix Halo), Radeon 8060S, 128 GB LPDDR5X |
| VRAM split | 96 GB dedicated carve in BIOS; Windows sees 31.6 GB system RAM; HIP reports 110456 MiB usable (dedicated + shared) |
| OS | Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, Adrenalin driver 32.0.31041.1004 |
| ROCm | TheRock wheels `rocm==10.0.0` with `libraries`, `device-gfx1151`, `devel` extras (HIP 7.15.26333, AMD clang 23.0.0 targeting `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`) |
| Build tools | Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC libs + rc.exe), CMake 4.2, ninja 1.13.2 (pip) |
| Model | unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (87.24 GiB, 3 shards) + EasiiX MTP sidecar Q8_0, both on the OS NVMe |

## Toolchain setup

The whole ROCm SDK comes from pip - no HIP SDK installer, no container. The
wheels are built by AMD's open-source
[TheRock](https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock) project (the same lineage as the
"TheRock 7.14 container stack" the Linux numbers were measured on) and served
from AMD's official wheel index:

```powershell
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[libraries,device-gfx1151]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[devel]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install ninja
```

The wheels land in `<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_*`. `rocm-sdk path --cmake`
prints the CMake package directory; it errors until the `devel` extra is
installed (the runtime-only `rocm` package has hipcc and clang but no CMake
configs). hipBLASLt ships in the Windows wheels, so `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1`
works.

Visual Studio 2022 is required for the MSVC runtime libraries and rc.exe.
One gotcha on this box: `vcvars64.bat` failed to set up the environment
(vswhere.exe not on PATH, rc.exe never resolved). `Launch-VsDevShell.ps1`
works:

```powershell
& "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Professional\Common7\Tools\Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
```

## Build

```powershell
# recommended: the measured Linux builds carry this correctness workaround too
git apply docs\strix-halo\llama-cpp-25992-rocm-host-buffer.patch
# (the per-buffer mmap patch no longer applies - expected, see Dockerfile.rocm-7.14)

$rocm = "<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_devel"
$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<env>\Scripts;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build
```

Clean build: 656 targets, zero errors, a handful of benign warnings (httplib
`ssize_t` extension, subprocess.h anonymous structs). The `AMDGPU_TARGETS is
deprecated` warning from hip-config is harmless (`GPU_TARGETS` is the new
name). `-DLLAMA_CURL=OFF` avoids a libcurl dev dependency; OpenSSL is also
not found, which only disables HTTPS in llama-server.

Verify the backend:

```
> llama-cli --list-devices
ROCm0: AMD Radeon(TM) 8060S Graphics (110456 MiB, 110301 MiB free)
Device 0: gfx1151 (0x1151), VMM: no, Wave Size: 32
```

## Running

The ROCm DLL directories must be on PATH at runtime:

```powershell
$sp = "<env>\Lib\site-packages"
$env:PATH = "$sp\_rocm_sdk_core\bin;$sp\_rocm_sdk_libraries\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf `
  -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -lzm on -c 163840 -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 `
  --parallel 1 --jinja --no-webui `
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0.gguf `
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod --spec-draft-n-max 4 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75
```

**Vision:** the model is multimodal but the quantized GGUFs ship the vision
encoder separately - without `--mmproj` any image input gets a 500 (`image
input is not supported`), which Claude Code hits whenever it reads a
screenshot. `mmproj-F16.gguf` (0.84 GiB) is in the same unsloth repo.
Verified working through `/v1/messages` (base64 image block described
correctly), coexisting with the MTP sidecar.

**Flag rename:** the `--tensor-read-lazy` flag named in README.md does not
exist on the current rebase - it is `-lzm` / `--lazy-mode on|auto|off` now.
As before, `auto` (the default) already covers the engram tensor, so `on`
only makes the intent explicit.

The `model has unused tensor blk.48.indexer.*` warnings at load come from the
MTP sidecar and are benign.

## Using it with Claude Code

Two things are needed; both verified working on 2026-09-02.

**1. The fixed chat template.** The official Qwen 3.8 template raises
`System message must be at the beginning` on mid-conversation system messages,
which agent tools send constantly - every such request is a 500. The
community-fixed template
[froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates](https://huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates)
(`qwen3.8-froggeric-v22.4`, the root `chat_template.jinja`) merges leading
system/developer messages and renders mid-conversation ones instead of
raising. Pass it with `--chat-template-file <path>\chat_template.jinja`.

**2. The native Anthropic endpoint.** This llama-server has an
Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint (with Claude Code-specific
system-prompt normalization in `tools/server/server-chat.cpp`), so no
OpenAI-translation proxy is needed - point Claude Code straight at it:

```powershell
$env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:7070"
$env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "none"
$env:CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW = "150000"
$env:CLAUDE_BYTE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:API_TIMEOUT_MS = "2400000"
claude --model qwen3.8-flash-next
```

The timeout overrides matter at this prefill speed: Claude Code always
streams and aborts a stream that stays silent for 5 minutes (byte- and
event-level watchdogs, defaults 300s, Claude Code 2.1.217+ behavior), then
retries automatically - a deep-context prefill (~12 min at 156K) would abort
and re-prefill in a loop that looks like a permanent "Waiting for API
response". 1800000 ms (30 min) is the documented cap for the idle watchdogs.
The retry logic itself is not configurable.

The model name is free-form - the server ignores it and always serves the
loaded model; pick something readable for the status line. The compact window
matters: Claude Code assumes a 200K context for unknown model names, but the
server slot is 163840 and a request beyond it is rejected with
`exceed_context_size_error` (context-shift is off by default). 150000 leaves
headroom for the response tokens and for the compaction request itself.
The env var name is version-dependent - if the limit shown by `/context`
does not change, compact manually before ~150K instead.

Verified with the fixed template loaded: mid-conversation system messages
return 200; a Claude Code-shaped `/v1/messages` request (system blocks + tool
definitions) returns a correct `tool_use` block with `stop_reason: tool_use`;
and the full round trip (`tool_use` -> `tool_result` -> final answer) works,
reasoning included.

Notes on a circulating Linux example for the same setup: its
`--tensor-read-lazy hangs indefinitely` warning comes from an
`HSA_XNACK=1`/`HSA_ENABLE_SDMA=0` stack (the Known-limits report in
README.md) - on this Windows build `-lzm on` runs clean, keep it. The
`HSA_*` variables themselves do not exist on Windows. Its other two warnings
match this branch's own guidance: never bf16 KV (use `q8_0`), and
`--parallel 1` only unless you built with the #25992 patch and accept the
unvalidated multi-slot path.

## LAN access

Bind to all interfaces and require a key - the server ships with CORS wide
open and no auth, do not expose it bare:

```
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 7070 --api-key <key>
```

(7070 here because 8080 tends to collide with other services.) Verified:
requests without the key get 401, with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` they
pass. Windows Firewall needs an inbound rule (admin PowerShell):

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "llama-server 7070" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 7070 -Action Allow -Profile Private,Domain
```

Claude Code on a client machine then uses the server's LAN IP with
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` set to the key. If Tailscale runs on both ends, the
tailnet IP works without touching the firewall and is the safer route off-LAN.

## Memory configuration

The 96 GB carve is what makes IQ4_XS fit: the GPU part is 60.4 GiB and the
Linux measurement puts a 262K-context load at 71.1 GiB - more than a 64 GB
carve, and spilling into WDDM shared memory is not something you want to
benchmark through. The cost of 96/32 is that `-lm none` (RAM mode) is off the
table: the 26.8 GiB engram table does not fit in 31.6 GB of system RAM, and
neither does a page cache large enough to hold it. If your workload is
short-context interactive and you want RAM mode with IQ3_XXS, use a 64/64
split instead - the two splits lock in different configurations.

## System RAM footprint while serving

Measured mid-session (96/32 split, 50K+ conversation cached): Windows shows
~26 GiB of the 31.6 GiB in use. Breakdown:

| | resident RAM |
|---|---|
| llama-server | 17.7 GiB |
| OS + everything else | ~8 GiB |
| available | 5.6 GiB |

The 17.7 GiB splits into roughly three kinds:

* **Hard private memory, ~8-11 GiB**: the server-side prompt cache
  (`--cache-ram`, default cap 8192 MiB - this is what buys incremental
  prefill), the resident engram lazy pages (~1-1.5 GiB), and host staging
  buffers. Shrinkable with `-cram 4096` at the cost of fewer cached states.
* **Reclaimable mapped file pages**: weight/engram pages touched during load.
  With drop-behind inert on Windows they stay in the working set, but they
  are clean pages - the memory manager evicts them on demand; the only cost
  is engram re-reads from SSD (slower prefill) afterwards.
* Its "private bytes" reads ~80 GiB, but that is WDDM charging the GPU
  allocations (the 96 GB carve) to the process - it does not live in the
  31.6 GiB, and the pagefile confirms it (1.6 GiB actually used). Commit
  looks near the limit (104/108 GiB) but the pagefile is system-managed and
  grows on demand.

Practical reading: other programs up to ~10 GiB run fine alongside (5.6 GiB
free plus evictable pages); at 20 GiB+ the prompt cache starts paging and
both sides crawl - stop the server or switch to a 64/64 split for that.

## What behaves differently on Windows

* `llama_mmap::prefetch_rows()` uses `PrefetchVirtualMemory` instead of
  `posix_madvise(WILLNEED)` - already implemented in the branch, nothing to do.
* `LLAMA_MMAP_DROP_BEHIND` is inert: `unmap_fragment()` is a no-op on Windows
  (a `MapViewOfFile` view cannot be partially unmapped) and there is no
  `posix_fadvise`. The load-phase page-cache peak documented in README.md is
  therefore not reduced; in practice the Windows standby-list reclaim absorbed
  it and the load went through without stalls.
* The Linux host prerequisites (kernel args, GTT sizing, TuneD) have no
  Windows equivalent; the BIOS VRAM carve replaces them.
* The `HSA_XNACK` lazy-read hang from Known limits is a Linux page-fault-path
  issue and cannot occur here.
* A Windows Defender exclusion on the model directory made no measurable
  difference (tested before/after with a server restart in between).

## Measured results (2026-09-02)

Server timings, temperature 0, q8_0 KV, `-c 163840`, MTP sidecar +
`draft-mtp,ngram-mod`, SSD mmap mode, hipBLASLt on. Fresh real-code prompts
per the BENCHMARKS.md methodology (warm-up request first; measured runs on
prompts the server has not seen).

| | Windows (this doc) | Linux reference (BENCHMARKS.md, IQ4_XS) |
|---|---|---|
| model load to listening | 1m28s-1m34s | "seconds" (mmap) |
| decode, code, MTP combo | **30.1-30.7 t/s**, 89.2% acceptance | 31.1 t/s |
| decode, cold first request | 28.1-30.4 t/s | (cold reads 20-55% low) |
| prefill @ ~4.4K depth, lazy SSD | **277.6-283.6 t/s** (4 runs, 2 sessions) | 395.6 t/s (IQ3 @4K; IQ4 llama-bench pp4096: 501.6 warm) |
| plain decode tail after prefill | 21.3-25.1 t/s | ~19-21 t/s @16-20K |

**llama-bench pair (2026-09-03, BENCHMARKS.md methodology, same flags):**

| test | Windows | Linux (IQ4_XS, warm cache) |
|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 | 314.05 +/- 52.35 | 501.6 |
| tg128 @ d0 | **22.77 +/- 0.18** | 22.8 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 258.79 +/- 2.56 | 379.3 |
| tg128 @ d16384 | **19.44 +/- 0.18** | 20.1 |

Reading: decode matches Linux to within noise at both depths - the
bandwidth-bound path is at full parity (same LPDDR5X). Prefill sits at 63-68%
of Linux even in llama-bench, i.e. **the gap is in the compute path, not in
the server or the SSD-lazy machinery** (earlier suspicion of
`PrefetchVirtualMemory`/page-cache effects is largely ruled out for this
metric). WDDM launch overhead is also a poor fit - decode issues far more
kernel launches per token and shows no gap. The pattern
(compute-throughput-bound path slow, bandwidth-bound path at parity) points
at sustained GPU compute clocks / power limits: the Linux box ran the TuneD
`accelerator-performance` profile, while this Windows box measured on the
default Balanced power plan.

**Elimination series (2026-09-03, all on the same llama-bench command):**

| variable toggled | pp4096 @ d0 | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Windows power slider Balanced -> Best Performance | 314 -> 308 (noise) | no effect |
| EVO-X2 front-panel P-mode -> Performance (red) | -> 322 (noise) | no effect - prefill is not power-limited here |
| `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT` on vs off, warm pages | **350.8** vs 341.3 (+/-0.5) | engaged and worth +2.8% - not the gap |
| BIOS Main -> Power Mode Select: Balance -> Performance | 345.2 warm, 258.9 @16K | no effect (16K identical to +/-0.01) |

The warm-state pp4096 @ d0 is 350.8 t/s (the mixed cold/warm runs above read
lower because the first rep pays cold engram reads - +/-50 variance), so the
honest warm-vs-warm ratio against Linux's 501.6 is 70%. With SSD-lazy,
server, and hipBLASLt all eliminated, decode at exact parity, and all three
power levers (Windows slider, front-panel P-mode, BIOS Power Mode Select)
proven no-ops, the last two suspects were the driver's compute clock policy
and device codegen. HWiNFO telemetry settled it: **during llama-bench
prefill the GPU sustains ~2.8 GHz (max ~2.9) while delivering ~339 t/s** -
the clock is fine, so the kernels are doing less work per clock than the
Linux build. Power telemetry agrees: APU STAPM sits at ~34% of its limit
(~40-50 W) during prefill - the chip is nowhere near a power wall, so
power-unlock tools (RyzenAdj etc.) have nothing to unlock here. (An earlier 1.6-1.8 GHz reading was taken under mixed
server/decode load, where low clocks are normal DVFS and harmless.)
A ubatch sweep (2048/4096/8192) moved nothing: warm pp4096 stays in the
340-360 band at every size.

### Toolchain A/B: building against ROCm 7.14 on Windows, step by step

Goal: rebuild the identical tree against the same ROCm generation the Linux
container uses (7.14) to test whether the newer toolchain caused the prefill
gap. Getting 7.14 onto Windows has some traps; the full path taken on
2026-09-04:

**1. Finding a 7.14 distribution.** The stable pip index
(`stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/`) carries exactly one version (10.0.0),
and TheRock's RELEASES.md states that 7.14 nightlies live only on the legacy
per-family index. Versions there are listed by
`pip index versions rocm --index-url https://rocm.nightlies.amd.com/v2/gfx1151/`;
the last 7.14 build is `7.14.0a20260612`.

**2. The pip route is broken - do not use it.** Installing
`rocm[libraries,devel]==7.14.0a20260612` from that index succeeds, but the
7.14-era devel wheel needs a manual `rocm-sdk init`, and on Windows that
expands 4.5 GB of *test binaries* into `_rocm_sdk_devel\bin` with empty
`include/`, `lib/`, and `cmake/` directories - no headers, no
`hip-config.cmake`, nothing to build against. (The 10.0.0 stable devel wheel
is fine; only the legacy nightly one is broken.)

**3. Use the TheRock tarball instead** (the same source lemonade's builds
use). Naming pattern `therock-dist-windows-<gfx>-<version>.tar.gz`;
availability can be probed with a HEAD request:

```powershell
curl.exe -sI https://therock-nightly-tarball.s3.amazonaws.com/therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0a20260612.tar.gz
# HTTP 200, ~2.5 GB
curl.exe -sL -o therock-714.tar.gz https://therock-nightly-tarball.s3.amazonaws.com/therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0a20260612.tar.gz
mkdir C:\opt\rocm714
tar -xzf therock-714.tar.gz -C C:\opt\rocm714
```

The tarball has the classic layout: `lib\cmake\` with all package configs,
`lib\llvm\bin\` with clang/clang++, runtime DLLs in `bin\`.

**4. Configure and build** - same recipe as the main build, only the paths
and a separate build directory change:

```powershell
& "C:\...\Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
$rocm = "C:\opt\rocm714"
$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<ninja dir>;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build-rocm714 -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build-rocm714 --target llama-bench   # ~15 min
```

**5. Run with the matching runtime.** The 7.14 binaries must load 7.14 DLLs -
put `C:\opt\rocm714\bin` first on PATH (not the 10.0 wheel directories):

```powershell
$env:PATH = "C:\opt\rocm714\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
# warm-up pass first (cold engram reads distort rep 1), then the measured pass:
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 16 -r 2
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2
```

**Result** (vs the 10.0-wheel build of the same tree, same day, same flags):

| | 7.14 tarball build | 10.0 wheel build |
|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 (warm rep) | ~345 | ~345-351 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 260.15 +/- 0.80 | 258.9 |
| tg128 / @16K | 22.33 / 19.10 | 22.7 / 19.4 |

Identical within noise - **the toolchain is exonerated**. Both SDKs ship
"AMD clang 23.0.0git", just different llvm-project snapshots (`52226beb` in
7.14 vs `8f497e09` in 10.0), and neither is the cause.
`GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` on the same build also changes nothing
(tg128 22.56 vs 22.3), so per-launch WDDM submission overhead is not the
story either.

**Final verdict (clock telemetry closed it):** correlated HWiNFO readings
show the two regimes directly - during heavy compute phases power rises to
~45 W and the GFX clock sits at **~1.8 GHz**, while the 2.6-2.8 GHz readings
occur in light phases at *lower* power. The GPU runs its GEMMs at ~1.8 GHz
by DVFS policy despite ~3x STAPM headroom: 1.8/2.9 = 62% of max clock,
which (plus small factors) accounts for the entire 69% prefill ratio.
The Linux reference pins this away - TuneD `accelerator-performance` forces
the amdgpu performance level high - while Adrenalin exposes no equivalent
control for the iGPU. So: not a bug in this branch, not the toolchain, not
power limits - a Windows driver DVFS policy for sustained compute, with no
known userspace override as of this writing. Decode, being bandwidth-bound,
is indifferent to it. Accept 70% prefill / 100% decode on Windows, or watch
Adrenalin releases for a compute/performance-level control.

### Real-workload statistics (Claude Code session, same day)

Aggregated from the server's `print_timing` lines over one evening of actual
Claude Code use against this server - 49 completed requests, conversation
depth growing past 50K tokens. Not a benchmark: mixed request sizes, mixed
content, one continuous session.

| | weighted average | per-request range |
|---|---|---|
| prefill | 196.7 t/s (131,429 tokens / 668 s) | 37.9 - 226.7 t/s |
| decode | 17.4 t/s (30,669 tokens / 1,760 s) | 12.4 - 26.3 t/s |
| MTP draft acceptance | 66.4% (19,821 / 29,854) | 40.0% - 92.3% |

Reading the numbers:

* The server-side prompt cache works: the full 50,623-token prefill happened
  once (cold start after a server restart, 223 s); every later turn prefilled
  only its delta (tens to a few thousand tokens). Per-turn wait is a few
  seconds to ~20 s of prefill plus generation.
* Decode below the 30 t/s short-context figure is the depth curve, not a
  Windows problem - at 50K+ depth the Linux reference is ~21 t/s MTP / ~13
  plain, which is exactly where these requests sit.
* Acceptance 66% average matches the Linux deep-context measurements (73.5%
  at 78K, 66% at 156K); the 40-56% outliers are free-form reasoning, the
  80-92% ones code.
* Low prefill t/s on tiny deltas (38 tokens at 37.9 t/s) is fixed overhead,
  under a second of absolute time.

Practical lever: keep working depth under ~30K (`/compact` early, fresh
sessions per task) and decode stays in the 20-25 t/s band.

Not measured on Windows: depth curves past 4.4K under controlled conditions,
llama-bench, PPL, multi-slot, RAM mode, the GDN chunk kernel
(`GGML_HIP_GDN_CHUNK=1`), and `test-qsa-gather-ms` (needs `--model`, not yet
run against the downloaded shards).

## Expert-pruned GSQ-RCO Coder vs IQ4_XS (2026-10-01)

[ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF)
is the same architecture with 256 of the 512 routed experts removed per layer
(RCO expert pruning) and the remaining weights at ~3.5 bpw (GSQ). The release
is code/agentic/vision targeted; the model card reports 91% of the base
SWE-bench Verified score and 99% of LiveCodeBench. Two shards, 58.4 GB total:
29.6 GB transformer (must be resident) + 28.8 GB engram table (IQ4_NL, same
lazy SSD path as the unsloth quants) + a 0.9 GB BF16 mmproj.

**Compatibility, checked before running:** `general.architecture = qwen4exp`,
`expert_count = 256`, `expert_used_count = 10`, and every hyper_connection /
ple / indexer / compress_ratios key this branch's loader reads is present. The
expert count comes from the metadata; nothing in the branch assumes 512. The
`IQ1_M` in the file name is a label only - the tensors are IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS /
IQ3_S / IQ4_NL / IQ4_XS / Q2_0 / Q4_K / Q5_K / Q6_K / Q8_0 / BF16 (per-tensor
map in `tensor-allocation/*.rco-allocation.txt`), all of which the HIP backend
has mmq / mmvq / getrows / convert kernels for. One difference from unsloth:
the router (`ffn_gate_inp`), `hc_*`, `ssm_alpha/beta` and `ple_key/value`
tensors are BF16 instead of F32 / Q8_0. It loads and runs on the build above
with no source change; the vision modality is reported on with the BF16
mmproj. Download note: this box has a wired default route; to pull over Wi-Fi
only, bind curl to the WLAN address (`curl.exe --interface <wlan-ip> -L -C -`).

**Procedure:** both models measured back to back on the same day, same

# Building and running on Windows 11 (gfx1151, TheRock ROCm wheels)

First Windows build of this branch, 2026-09-02. Summary: **no source changes were
needed** - the branch compiles and runs as-is with the TheRock ROCm SDK for
Windows. MTP decode reaches parity with the Linux numbers (30.1-30.7 t/s code
vs 31.1 in BENCHMARKS.md); prefill lands at ~71% of the Linux SSD-lazy rate
(278-284 t/s at 4.4K depth vs 396). Single machine, single day of measurements -
treat everything below as n=1.

## Test machine

| | |
|---|---|
| System | AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 (Strix Halo), Radeon 8060S, 128 GB LPDDR5X |
| VRAM split | 96 GB dedicated carve in BIOS; Windows sees 31.6 GB system RAM; HIP reports 110456 MiB usable (dedicated + shared) |
| OS | Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, Adrenalin driver 32.0.31041.1004 |
| ROCm | TheRock wheels `rocm==10.0.0` with `libraries`, `device-gfx1151`, `devel` extras (HIP 7.15.26333, AMD clang 23.0.0 targeting `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`) |
| Build tools | Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC libs + rc.exe), CMake 4.2, ninja 1.13.2 (pip) |
| Model | unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (87.24 GiB, 3 shards) + EasiiX MTP sidecar Q8_0, both on the OS NVMe |

## Toolchain setup

The whole ROCm SDK comes from pip - no HIP SDK installer, no container. The
wheels are built by AMD's open-source
[TheRock](https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock) project (the same lineage as the
"TheRock 7.14 container stack" the Linux numbers were measured on) and served
from AMD's official wheel index:

```powershell
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[libraries,device-gfx1151]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[devel]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install ninja
```

The wheels land in `<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_*`. `rocm-sdk path --cmake`
prints the CMake package directory; it errors until the `devel` extra is
installed (the runtime-only `rocm` package has hipcc and clang but no CMake
configs). hipBLASLt ships in the Windows wheels, so `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1`
works.

Visual Studio 2022 is required for the MSVC runtime libraries and rc.exe.
One gotcha on this box: `vcvars64.bat` failed to set up the environment
(vswhere.exe not on PATH, rc.exe never resolved). `Launch-VsDevShell.ps1`
works:

```powershell
& "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Professional\Common7\Tools\Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
```

## Build

```powershell
# recommended: the measured Linux builds carry this correctness workaround too
git apply docs\strix-halo\llama-cpp-25992-rocm-host-buffer.patch
# (the per-buffer mmap patch no longer applies - expected, see Dockerfile.rocm-7.14)

$rocm = "<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_devel"
$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<env>\Scripts;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build
```

Clean build: 656 targets, zero errors, a handful of benign warnings (httplib
`ssize_t` extension, subprocess.h anonymous structs). The `AMDGPU_TARGETS is
deprecated` warning from hip-config is harmless (`GPU_TARGETS` is the new
name). `-DLLAMA_CURL=OFF` avoids a libcurl dev dependency; OpenSSL is also
not found, which only disables HTTPS in llama-server.

Verify the backend:

```
> llama-cli --list-devices
ROCm0: AMD Radeon(TM) 8060S Graphics (110456 MiB, 110301 MiB free)
Device 0: gfx1151 (0x1151), VMM: no, Wave Size: 32
```

## Running

The ROCm DLL directories must be on PATH at runtime:

```powershell
$sp = "<env>\Lib\site-packages"
$env:PATH = "$sp\_rocm_sdk_core\bin;$sp\_rocm_sdk_libraries\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf `
  -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -lzm on -c 163840 -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 `
  --parallel 1 --jinja --no-webui `
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0.gguf `
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod --spec-draft-n-max 4 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75
```

**Vision:** the model is multimodal but the quantized GGUFs ship the vision
encoder separately - without `--mmproj` any image input gets a 500 (`image
input is not supported`), which Claude Code hits whenever it reads a
screenshot. `mmproj-F16.gguf` (0.84 GiB) is in the same unsloth repo.
Verified working through `/v1/messages` (base64 image block described
correctly), coexisting with the MTP sidecar.

**Flag rename:** the `--tensor-read-lazy` flag named in README.md does not
exist on the current rebase - it is `-lzm` / `--lazy-mode on|auto|off` now.
As before, `auto` (the default) already covers the engram tensor, so `on`
only makes the intent explicit.

The `model has unused tensor blk.48.indexer.*` warnings at load come from the
MTP sidecar and are benign.

## Using it with Claude Code

Two things are needed; both verified working on 2026-09-02.

**1. The fixed chat template.** The official Qwen 3.8 template raises
`System message must be at the beginning` on mid-conversation system messages,
which agent tools send constantly - every such request is a 500. The
community-fixed template
[froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates](https://huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates)
(`qwen3.8-froggeric-v22.4`, the root `chat_template.jinja`) merges leading
system/developer messages and renders mid-conversation ones instead of
raising. Pass it with `--chat-template-file <path>\chat_template.jinja`.

**2. The native Anthropic endpoint.** This llama-server has an
Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint (with Claude Code-specific
system-prompt normalization in `tools/server/server-chat.cpp`), so no
OpenAI-translation proxy is needed - point Claude Code straight at it:

```powershell
$env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:7070"
$env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "none"
$env:CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW = "150000"
$env:CLAUDE_BYTE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:API_TIMEOUT_MS = "2400000"
claude --model qwen3.8-flash-next
```

The timeout overrides matter at this prefill speed: Claude Code always
streams and aborts a stream that stays silent for 5 minutes (byte- and
event-level watchdogs, defaults 300s, Claude Code 2.1.217+ behavior), then
retries automatically - a deep-context prefill (~12 min at 156K) would abort
and re-prefill in a loop that looks like a permanent "Waiting for API
response". 1800000 ms (30 min) is the documented cap for the idle watchdogs.
The retry logic itself is not configurable.

The model name is free-form - the server ignores it and always serves the
loaded model; pick something readable for the status line. The compact window
matters: Claude Code assumes a 200K context for unknown model names, but the
server slot is 163840 and a request beyond it is rejected with
`exceed_context_size_error` (context-shift is off by default). 150000 leaves
headroom for the response tokens and for the compaction request itself.
The env var name is version-dependent - if the limit shown by `/context`
does not change, compact manually before ~150K instead.

Verified with the fixed template loaded: mid-conversation system messages
return 200; a Claude Code-shaped `/v1/messages` request (system blocks + tool
definitions) returns a correct `tool_use` block with `stop_reason: tool_use`;
and the full round trip (`tool_use` -> `tool_result` -> final answer) works,
reasoning included.

Notes on a circulating Linux example for the same setup: its
`--tensor-read-lazy hangs indefinitely` warning comes from an
`HSA_XNACK=1`/`HSA_ENABLE_SDMA=0` stack (the Known-limits report in
README.md) - on this Windows build `-lzm on` runs clean, keep it. The
`HSA_*` variables themselves do not exist on Windows. Its other two warnings
match this branch's own guidance: never bf16 KV (use `q8_0`), and
`--parallel 1` only unless you built with the #25992 patch and accept the
unvalidated multi-slot path.

## LAN access

Bind to all interfaces and require a key - the server ships with CORS wide
open and no auth, do not expose it bare:

```
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 7070 --api-key <key>
```

(7070 here because 8080 tends to collide with other services.) Verified:
requests without the key get 401, with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` they
pass. Windows Firewall needs an inbound rule (admin PowerShell):

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "llama-server 7070" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 7070 -Action Allow -Profile Private,Domain
```

Claude Code on a client machine then uses the server's LAN IP with
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` set to the key. If Tailscale runs on both ends, the
tailnet IP works without touching the firewall and is the safer route off-LAN.

## Memory configuration

The 96 GB carve is what makes IQ4_XS fit: the GPU part is 60.4 GiB and the
Linux measurement puts a 262K-context load at 71.1 GiB - more than a 64 GB
carve, and spilling into WDDM shared memory is not something you want to
benchmark through. The cost of 96/32 is that `-lm none` (RAM mode) is off the
table: the 26.8 GiB engram table does not fit in 31.6 GB of system RAM, and
neither does a page cache large enough to hold it. If your workload is
short-context interactive and you want RAM mode with IQ3_XXS, use a 64/64
split instead - the two splits lock in different configurations.

## System RAM footprint while serving

Measured mid-session (96/32 split, 50K+ conversation cached): Windows shows
~26 GiB of the 31.6 GiB in use. Breakdown:

| | resident RAM |
|---|---|
| llama-server | 17.7 GiB |
| OS + everything else | ~8 GiB |
| available | 5.6 GiB |

The 17.7 GiB splits into roughly three kinds:

* **Hard private memory, ~8-11 GiB**: the server-side prompt cache
  (`--cache-ram`, default cap 8192 MiB - this is what buys incremental
  prefill), the resident engram lazy pages (~1-1.5 GiB), and host staging
  buffers. Shrinkable with `-cram 4096` at the cost of fewer cached states.
* **Reclaimable mapped file pages**: weight/engram pages touched during load.
  With drop-behind inert on Windows they stay in the working set, but they
  are clean pages - the memory manager evicts them on demand; the only cost
  is engram re-reads from SSD (slower prefill) afterwards.
* Its "private bytes" reads ~80 GiB, but that is WDDM charging the GPU
  allocations (the 96 GB carve) to the process - it does not live in the
  31.6 GiB, and the pagefile confirms it (1.6 GiB actually used). Commit
  looks near the limit (104/108 GiB) but the pagefile is system-managed and
  grows on demand.

Practical reading: other programs up to ~10 GiB run fine alongside (5.6 GiB
free plus evictable pages); at 20 GiB+ the prompt cache starts paging and
both sides crawl - stop the server or switch to a 64/64 split for that.

## What behaves differently on Windows

* `llama_mmap::prefetch_rows()` uses `PrefetchVirtualMemory` instead of
  `posix_madvise(WILLNEED)` - already implemented in the branch, nothing to do.
* `LLAMA_MMAP_DROP_BEHIND` is inert: `unmap_fragment()` is a no-op on Windows
  (a `MapViewOfFile` view cannot be partially unmapped) and there is no
  `posix_fadvise`. The load-phase page-cache peak documented in README.md is
  therefore not reduced; in practice the Windows standby-list reclaim absorbed
  it and the load went through without stalls.
* The Linux host prerequisites (kernel args, GTT sizing, TuneD) have no
  Windows equivalent; the BIOS VRAM carve replaces them.
* The `HSA_XNACK` lazy-read hang from Known limits is a Linux page-fault-path
  issue and cannot occur here.
* A Windows Defender exclusion on the model directory made no measurable
  difference (tested before/after with a server restart in between).

Server timings, temperature 0, q8_0 KV, `-c 163840`, MTP sidecar +
`draft-mtp,ngram-mod`, SSD mmap mode, hipBLASLt on. Fresh real-code prompts
per the BENCHMARKS.md methodology (warm-up request first; measured runs on
prompts the server has not seen).

| | Windows (this doc) | Linux reference (BENCHMARKS.md, IQ4_XS) |

**llama-bench pair (2026-09-03, BENCHMARKS.md methodology, same flags):**

| test | Windows | Linux (IQ4_XS, warm cache) |

| pp4096 @ d0 | 314.05 +/- 52.35 | 501.6 |
| tg128 @ d0 | **22.77 +/- 0.18** | 22.8 |

bandwidth-bound path is at full parity (same LPDDR5X). Prefill sits at 63-68%

the server or the SSD-lazy machinery** (earlier suspicion of

metric). WDDM launch overhead is also a poor fit - decode issues far more

**Elimination series (2026-09-03, all on the same llama-bench command):**

| variable toggled | pp4096 @ d0 | verdict |

A ubatch sweep (2048/4096/8192) moved nothing: warm pp4096 stays in the
340-360 band at every size.

### Toolchain A/B: building against ROCm 7.14 on Windows, step by step

Goal: rebuild the identical tree against the same ROCm generation the Linux
container uses (7.14) to test whether the newer toolchain caused the prefill
gap. Getting 7.14 onto Windows has some traps; the full path taken on
2026-09-04:

**1. Finding a 7.14 distribution.** The stable pip index
(`stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/`) carries exactly one version (10.0.0),
and TheRock's RELEASES.md states that 7.14 nightlies live only on the legacy
per-family index. Versions there are listed by
`pip index versions rocm --index-url https://rocm.nightlies.amd.com/v2/gfx1151/`;
the last 7.14 build is `7.14.0a20260612`.

**2. The pip route is broken - do not use it.** Installing
`rocm[libraries,devel]==7.14.0a20260612` from that index succeeds, but the
7.14-era devel wheel needs a manual `rocm-sdk init`, and on Windows that
expands 4.5 GB of *test binaries* into `_rocm_sdk_devel\bin` with empty
`include/`, `lib/`, and `cmake/` directories - no headers, no
`hip-config.cmake`, nothing to build against. (The 10.0.0 stable devel wheel
is fine; only the legacy nightly one is broken.)

**3. Use the TheRock tarball instead** (the same source lemonade's builds
use). Naming pattern `therock-dist-windows-<gfx>-<version>.tar.gz`;
availability can be probed with a HEAD request:

```powershell

curl.exe -sL -o therock-714.tar.gz https://therock-nightly-tarball.s3.amazonaws.com/therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0a20260612.tar.gz
mkdir C:\opt\rocm714
tar -xzf therock-714.tar.gz -C C:\opt\rocm714
```

The tarball has the classic layout: `lib\cmake\` with all package configs,
`lib\llvm\bin\` with clang/clang++, runtime DLLs in `bin\`.

**4. Configure and build** - same recipe as the main build, only the paths
and a separate build directory change:

```powershell

$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<ninja dir>;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build-rocm714 -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build-rocm714 --target llama-bench   # ~15 min
```

**5. Run with the matching runtime.** The 7.14 binaries must load 7.14 DLLs -
put `C:\opt\rocm714\bin` first on PATH (not the 10.0 wheel directories):

```powershell
$env:PATH = "C:\opt\rocm714\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
# warm-up pass first (cold engram reads distort rep 1), then the measured pass:
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 16 -r 2
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2
```

**Result** (vs the 10.0-wheel build of the same tree, same day, same flags):

| | 7.14 tarball build | 10.0 wheel build |
|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 (warm rep) | ~345 | ~345-351 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 260.15 +/- 0.80 | 258.9 |
| tg128 / @16K | 22.33 / 19.10 | 22.7 / 19.4 |

Identical within noise - **the toolchain is exonerated**. Both SDKs ship
"AMD clang 23.0.0git", just different llvm-project snapshots (`52226beb` in
7.14 vs `8f497e09` in 10.0), and neither is the cause.
`GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` on the same build also changes nothing
(tg128 22.56 vs 22.3), so per-launch WDDM submission overhead is not the
story either.

**Final verdict (clock telemetry closed it):** correlated HWiNFO readings
show the two regimes directly - during heavy compute phases power rises to
~45 W and the GFX clock sits at **~1.8 GHz**, while the 2.6-2.8 GHz readings
occur in light phases at *lower* power. The GPU runs its GEMMs at ~1.8 GHz
by DVFS policy despite ~3x STAPM headroom: 1.8/2.9 = 62% of max clock,
which (plus small factors) accounts for the entire 69% prefill ratio.
The Linux reference pins this away - TuneD `accelerator-performance` forces
the amdgpu performance level high - while Adrenalin exposes no equivalent
control for the iGPU. So: not a bug in this branch, not the toolchain, not
power limits - a Windows driver DVFS policy for sustained compute, with no
known userspace override as of this writing. Decode, being bandwidth-bound,
is indifferent to it. Accept 70% prefill / 100% decode on Windows, or watch
Adrenalin releases for a compute/performance-level control.

### Real-workload statistics (Claude Code session, same day)

Aggregated from the server's `print_timing` lines over one evening of actual
Claude Code use against this server - 49 completed requests, conversation
depth growing past 50K tokens. Not a benchmark: mixed request sizes, mixed
content, one continuous session.

| | weighted average | per-request range |
|---|---|---|
| prefill | 196.7 t/s (131,429 tokens / 668 s) | 37.9 - 226.7 t/s |
| decode | 17.4 t/s (30,669 tokens / 1,760 s) | 12.4 - 26.3 t/s |
| MTP draft acceptance | 66.4% (19,821 / 29,854) | 40.0% - 92.3% |

Reading the numbers:

* The server-side prompt cache works: the full 50,623-token prefill happened
  once (cold start after a server restart, 223 s); every later turn prefilled
  only its delta (tens to a few thousand tokens). Per-turn wait is a few
  seconds to ~20 s of prefill plus generation.
* Decode below the 30 t/s short-context figure is the depth curve, not a
  Windows problem - at 50K+ depth the Linux reference is ~21 t/s MTP / ~13
  plain, which is exactly where these requests sit.
* Acceptance 66% average matches the Linux deep-context measurements (73.5%
  at 78K, 66% at 156K); the 40-56% outliers are free-form reasoning, the
  80-92% ones code.
* Low prefill t/s on tiny deltas (38 tokens at 37.9 t/s) is fixed overhead,
  under a second of absolute time.

Practical lever: keep working depth under ~30K (`/compact` early, fresh
sessions per task) and decode stays in the 20-25 t/s band.

Not measured on Windows: depth curves past 4.4K under controlled conditions,
llama-bench, PPL, multi-slot, RAM mode, the GDN chunk kernel
(`GGML_HIP_GDN_CHUNK=1`), and `test-qsa-gather-ms` (needs `--model`, not yet
run against the downloaded shards).

## Expert-pruned GSQ-RCO Coder vs IQ4_XS (2026-10-01)

[ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF)
is the same architecture with 256 of the 512 routed experts removed per layer
(RCO expert pruning) and the remaining weights at ~3.5 bpw (GSQ). The release
is code/agentic/vision targeted; the model card reports 91% of the base
SWE-bench Verified score and 99% of LiveCodeBench. Two shards, 58.4 GB total:
29.6 GB transformer (must be resident) + 28.8 GB engram table (IQ4_NL, same
lazy SSD path as the unsloth quants) + a 0.9 GB BF16 mmproj.

**Compatibility, checked before running:** `general.architecture = qwen4exp`,
`expert_count = 256`, `expert_used_count = 10`, and every hyper_connection /
ple / indexer / compress_ratios key this branch's loader reads is present. The
expert count comes from the metadata; nothing in the branch assumes 512. The
`IQ1_M` in the file name is a label only - the tensors are IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS /
IQ3_S / IQ4_NL / IQ4_XS / Q2_0 / Q4_K / Q5_K / Q6_K / Q8_0 / BF16 (per-tensor
map in `tensor-allocation/*.rco-allocation.txt`), all of which the HIP backend
has mmq / mmvq / getrows / convert kernels for. One difference from unsloth:
the router (`ffn_gate_inp`), `hc_*`, `ssm_alpha/beta` and `ple_key/value`
tensors are BF16 instead of F32 / Q8_0. It loads and runs on the build above
with no source change; the vision modality is reported on with the BF16
mmproj. Download note: this box has a wired default route; to pull over Wi-Fi
only, bind curl to the WLAN address (`curl.exe --interface <wlan-ip> -L -C -`).

**Procedure:** both models measured back to back on the same day, same
binary, same flags as the tables above, nothing else on the GPU. llama-bench:
one warm-up pass (`-p 4096 -n 16 -r 2`) then the measured pass
(`-p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2`). Server: `-c 163840`, q8_0 KV, `-lm mmap
-lzm on`, hipBLASLt on, the EasiiX MTP sidecar + `draft-mtp,ngram-mod` on both
(the sidecar is a separate draft model and does not depend on the target's
expert count), temperature 0, 400 tokens out, numbers from the `timings`
object. Request order per server: a short real-code prompt as cold first
request, a fresh short real-code prompt (measured decode), a ~4.75K-token
chunk of `llama-model-loader.cpp` (measured prefill + decode tail), then the
first prompt repeated (reference only - prompt cache and ngram have seen it).

**llama-bench pair:**

| test | GSQ-RCO Coder | IQ4_XS, same day | IQ4_XS, 2026-09-03 above |
|---|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 | 318.1 +/- 70.0 (warm-up pass: 365.3) | 339.5 +/- 6.0 (warm-up pass: 337.2) | 314.1 +/- 52.4 (warm 350.8) |
| tg128 @ d0 | 20.92 +/- 0.19 | 21.83 +/- 0.52 | 22.77 +/- 0.18 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | **269.9 +/- 1.2** | 244.1 +/- 19.5 | 258.8 +/- 2.6 |
| tg128 @ d16384 | 17.98 +/- 0.15 | 16.25 +/- 4.23 | 19.44 +/- 0.18 |

The IQ4_XS d16384 rows were noisy this day (+/-4 on tg128, below the
September numbers); treat the September column as the better IQ4_XS anchor
for those two cells. The +/-70 on the GSQ d0 prefill is the usual cold first
rep (engram reads), same as documented above.

**Server timings:**

| | GSQ-RCO Coder | IQ4_XS, same day | IQ4_XS, 2026-09-02 above |
|---|---|---|---|
| model load to listening | **30 s** | 83 s | 1m28s-1m34s |
| cold first request, decode (MTP) | 26.1 t/s, 86.5% acc | 28.2 t/s, 87.8% acc | 28.1-30.4 t/s |
| fresh code prompt, decode (MTP) | 21.9 t/s, 74.5% acc | 25.1 t/s, 78.2% acc | 30.1-30.7 t/s, 89.2% acc |
| prefill @ 4754 depth | **321.5 t/s** | 277.2 t/s | 277.6-283.6 t/s |
| decode tail after that prefill | 20.8 t/s, 81.9% acc | 23.0 t/s, 84.9% acc | 21.3-25.1 t/s |
| repeated prompt (reference only) | 49.9 t/s | 58.6 t/s, 99.2% acc | |

**Reading the numbers:**

* Pruning does not speed up decode. Decode is bandwidth-bound on the 10
  active experts per token, and that count is unchanged; the retained weights
  use IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS / Q2_0 types whose dequant costs more per byte than
  IQ4_XS, so decode lands ~5-10% below IQ4_XS at every depth.
* Prefill at depth is where the halved expert count shows: a batch touches
  every expert of a layer, so expert weight traffic halves and pp4096 @ 16K
  is +4% (vs the September anchor) to +10% (same day), the 4.75K server
  prefill +16%.
* Load time drops from ~85 s to 30 s and the on-disk footprint from 87 GiB to
  54 GiB (GPU-resident part ~30 GB vs 60 GB), which is the practical win: it
  fits a 64 GB carve with room for context.
* The fresh-prompt acceptance (74-78%) is lower than the September 89% on both
  models for a prompt reason, not a model one: the "fresh" prompt pasted a
  type-trait table instead of a function, both models correctly refused to
  rewrite it and answered in prose, and prose drafts worse than code. The
  comparison between the two models holds; the absolute number is not the
  code-decode figure of the earlier tables.
* No quality comparison yet: on the 4.75K prompt both models spent the whole
  400-token budget in reasoning, and the two short prompts were answered
  correctly by both. Quality vs IQ4_XS on real agent work is unmeasured.

# Building and running on Windows 11 (gfx1151, TheRock ROCm wheels)

First Windows build of this branch, 2026-09-02. Summary: **no source changes were
needed** - the branch compiles and runs as-is with the TheRock ROCm SDK for
Windows. MTP decode reaches parity with the Linux numbers (30.1-30.7 t/s code
vs 31.1 in BENCHMARKS.md); prefill lands at ~71% of the Linux SSD-lazy rate
(278-284 t/s at 4.4K depth vs 396). Single machine, single day of measurements -
treat everything below as n=1.

## Test machine

| | |
|---|---|
| System | AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 (Strix Halo), Radeon 8060S, 128 GB LPDDR5X |
| VRAM split | 96 GB dedicated carve in BIOS; Windows sees 31.6 GB system RAM; HIP reports 110456 MiB usable (dedicated + shared) |
| OS | Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, Adrenalin driver 32.0.31041.1004 |
| ROCm | TheRock wheels `rocm==10.0.0` with `libraries`, `device-gfx1151`, `devel` extras (HIP 7.15.26333, AMD clang 23.0.0 targeting `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`) |
| Build tools | Visual Studio 2022 (MSVC libs + rc.exe), CMake 4.2, ninja 1.13.2 (pip) |
| Model | unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (87.24 GiB, 3 shards) + EasiiX MTP sidecar Q8_0, both on the OS NVMe |

## Toolchain setup

The whole ROCm SDK comes from pip - no HIP SDK installer, no container. The
wheels are built by AMD's open-source
[TheRock](https://github.com/ROCm/TheRock) project (the same lineage as the
"TheRock 7.14 container stack" the Linux numbers were measured on) and served
from AMD's official wheel index:

```powershell
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[libraries,device-gfx1151]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install --index-url https://stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/ "rocm[devel]==10.0.0"
python -m pip install ninja
```

The wheels land in `<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_*`. `rocm-sdk path --cmake`
prints the CMake package directory; it errors until the `devel` extra is
installed (the runtime-only `rocm` package has hipcc and clang but no CMake
configs). hipBLASLt ships in the Windows wheels, so `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT=1`
works.

Visual Studio 2022 is required for the MSVC runtime libraries and rc.exe.
One gotcha on this box: `vcvars64.bat` failed to set up the environment
(vswhere.exe not on PATH, rc.exe never resolved). `Launch-VsDevShell.ps1`
works:

```powershell
& "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Professional\Common7\Tools\Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
```

## Build

```powershell
# recommended: the measured Linux builds carry this correctness workaround too
git apply docs\strix-halo\llama-cpp-25992-rocm-host-buffer.patch
# (the per-buffer mmap patch no longer applies - expected, see Dockerfile.rocm-7.14)

$rocm = "<env>\Lib\site-packages\_rocm_sdk_devel"
$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<env>\Scripts;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build
```

Clean build: 656 targets, zero errors, a handful of benign warnings (httplib
`ssize_t` extension, subprocess.h anonymous structs). The `AMDGPU_TARGETS is
deprecated` warning from hip-config is harmless (`GPU_TARGETS` is the new
name). `-DLLAMA_CURL=OFF` avoids a libcurl dev dependency; OpenSSL is also
not found, which only disables HTTPS in llama-server.

Verify the backend:

```
> llama-cli --list-devices
ROCm0: AMD Radeon(TM) 8060S Graphics (110456 MiB, 110301 MiB free)
Device 0: gfx1151 (0x1151), VMM: no, Wave Size: 32
```

## Running

The ROCm DLL directories must be on PATH at runtime:

```powershell
$sp = "<env>\Lib\site-packages"
$env:PATH = "$sp\_rocm_sdk_core\bin;$sp\_rocm_sdk_libraries\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf `
  -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -lzm on -c 163840 -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 `
  --parallel 1 --jinja --no-webui `
  -md mtp-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Q8_0.gguf `
  --mmproj mmproj-F16.gguf `
  --spec-type draft-mtp,ngram-mod --spec-draft-n-max 4 --spec-draft-p-min 0.75
```

**Vision:** the model is multimodal but the quantized GGUFs ship the vision
encoder separately - without `--mmproj` any image input gets a 500 (`image
input is not supported`), which Claude Code hits whenever it reads a
screenshot. `mmproj-F16.gguf` (0.84 GiB) is in the same unsloth repo.
Verified working through `/v1/messages` (base64 image block described
correctly), coexisting with the MTP sidecar.

**Flag rename:** the `--tensor-read-lazy` flag named in README.md does not
exist on the current rebase - it is `-lzm` / `--lazy-mode on|auto|off` now.
As before, `auto` (the default) already covers the engram tensor, so `on`
only makes the intent explicit.

The `model has unused tensor blk.48.indexer.*` warnings at load come from the
MTP sidecar and are benign.

## Using it with Claude Code

Two things are needed; both verified working on 2026-09-02.

**1. The fixed chat template.** The official Qwen 3.8 template raises
`System message must be at the beginning` on mid-conversation system messages,
which agent tools send constantly - every such request is a 500. The
community-fixed template
[froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates](https://huggingface.co/froggeric/Qwen-Fixed-Chat-Templates)
(`qwen3.8-froggeric-v22.4`, the root `chat_template.jinja`) merges leading
system/developer messages and renders mid-conversation ones instead of
raising. Pass it with `--chat-template-file <path>\chat_template.jinja`.

**2. The native Anthropic endpoint.** This llama-server has an
Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint (with Claude Code-specific
system-prompt normalization in `tools/server/server-chat.cpp`), so no
OpenAI-translation proxy is needed - point Claude Code straight at it:

```powershell
$env:ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:7070"
$env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "none"
$env:CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW = "150000"
$env:CLAUDE_BYTE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = "1800000"
$env:API_TIMEOUT_MS = "2400000"
claude --model qwen3.8-flash-next
```

The timeout overrides matter at this prefill speed: Claude Code always
streams and aborts a stream that stays silent for 5 minutes (byte- and
event-level watchdogs, defaults 300s, Claude Code 2.1.217+ behavior), then
retries automatically - a deep-context prefill (~12 min at 156K) would abort
and re-prefill in a loop that looks like a permanent "Waiting for API
response". 1800000 ms (30 min) is the documented cap for the idle watchdogs.
The retry logic itself is not configurable.

The model name is free-form - the server ignores it and always serves the
loaded model; pick something readable for the status line. The compact window
matters: Claude Code assumes a 200K context for unknown model names, but the
server slot is 163840 and a request beyond it is rejected with
`exceed_context_size_error` (context-shift is off by default). 150000 leaves
headroom for the response tokens and for the compaction request itself.
The env var name is version-dependent - if the limit shown by `/context`
does not change, compact manually before ~150K instead.

Verified with the fixed template loaded: mid-conversation system messages
return 200; a Claude Code-shaped `/v1/messages` request (system blocks + tool
definitions) returns a correct `tool_use` block with `stop_reason: tool_use`;
and the full round trip (`tool_use` -> `tool_result` -> final answer) works,
reasoning included.

Notes on a circulating Linux example for the same setup: its
`--tensor-read-lazy hangs indefinitely` warning comes from an
`HSA_XNACK=1`/`HSA_ENABLE_SDMA=0` stack (the Known-limits report in
README.md) - on this Windows build `-lzm on` runs clean, keep it. The
`HSA_*` variables themselves do not exist on Windows. Its other two warnings
match this branch's own guidance: never bf16 KV (use `q8_0`), and
`--parallel 1` only unless you built with the #25992 patch and accept the
unvalidated multi-slot path.

## LAN access

Bind to all interfaces and require a key - the server ships with CORS wide
open and no auth, do not expose it bare:

```
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 7070 --api-key <key>
```

(7070 here because 8080 tends to collide with other services.) Verified:
requests without the key get 401, with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` they
pass. Windows Firewall needs an inbound rule (admin PowerShell):

```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "llama-server 7070" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 7070 -Action Allow -Profile Private,Domain
```

Claude Code on a client machine then uses the server's LAN IP with
`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` set to the key. If Tailscale runs on both ends, the
tailnet IP works without touching the firewall and is the safer route off-LAN.

## Memory configuration

The 96 GB carve is what makes IQ4_XS fit: the GPU part is 60.4 GiB and the
Linux measurement puts a 262K-context load at 71.1 GiB - more than a 64 GB
carve, and spilling into WDDM shared memory is not something you want to
benchmark through. The cost of 96/32 is that `-lm none` (RAM mode) is off the
table: the 26.8 GiB engram table does not fit in 31.6 GB of system RAM, and
neither does a page cache large enough to hold it. If your workload is
short-context interactive and you want RAM mode with IQ3_XXS, use a 64/64
split instead - the two splits lock in different configurations.

## System RAM footprint while serving

Measured mid-session (96/32 split, 50K+ conversation cached): Windows shows
~26 GiB of the 31.6 GiB in use. Breakdown:

| | resident RAM |
|---|---|
| llama-server | 17.7 GiB |
| OS + everything else | ~8 GiB |
| available | 5.6 GiB |

The 17.7 GiB splits into roughly three kinds:

* **Hard private memory, ~8-11 GiB**: the server-side prompt cache
  (`--cache-ram`, default cap 8192 MiB - this is what buys incremental
  prefill), the resident engram lazy pages (~1-1.5 GiB), and host staging
  buffers. Shrinkable with `-cram 4096` at the cost of fewer cached states.
* **Reclaimable mapped file pages**: weight/engram pages touched during load.
  With drop-behind inert on Windows they stay in the working set, but they
  are clean pages - the memory manager evicts them on demand; the only cost
  is engram re-reads from SSD (slower prefill) afterwards.
* Its "private bytes" reads ~80 GiB, but that is WDDM charging the GPU
  allocations (the 96 GB carve) to the process - it does not live in the
  31.6 GiB, and the pagefile confirms it (1.6 GiB actually used). Commit
  looks near the limit (104/108 GiB) but the pagefile is system-managed and
  grows on demand.

Practical reading: other programs up to ~10 GiB run fine alongside (5.6 GiB
free plus evictable pages); at 20 GiB+ the prompt cache starts paging and
both sides crawl - stop the server or switch to a 64/64 split for that.

## What behaves differently on Windows

* `llama_mmap::prefetch_rows()` uses `PrefetchVirtualMemory` instead of
  `posix_madvise(WILLNEED)` - already implemented in the branch, nothing to do.
* `LLAMA_MMAP_DROP_BEHIND` is inert: `unmap_fragment()` is a no-op on Windows
  (a `MapViewOfFile` view cannot be partially unmapped) and there is no
  `posix_fadvise`. The load-phase page-cache peak documented in README.md is
  therefore not reduced; in practice the Windows standby-list reclaim absorbed
  it and the load went through without stalls.
* The Linux host prerequisites (kernel args, GTT sizing, TuneD) have no
  Windows equivalent; the BIOS VRAM carve replaces them.
* The `HSA_XNACK` lazy-read hang from Known limits is a Linux page-fault-path
  issue and cannot occur here.
* A Windows Defender exclusion on the model directory made no measurable
  difference (tested before/after with a server restart in between).

## Measured results (2026-09-02)

Server timings, temperature 0, q8_0 KV, `-c 163840`, MTP sidecar +
`draft-mtp,ngram-mod`, SSD mmap mode, hipBLASLt on. Fresh real-code prompts
per the BENCHMARKS.md methodology (warm-up request first; measured runs on
prompts the server has not seen).

| | Windows (this doc) | Linux reference (BENCHMARKS.md, IQ4_XS) |
|---|---|---|
| model load to listening | 1m28s-1m34s | "seconds" (mmap) |
| decode, code, MTP combo | **30.1-30.7 t/s**, 89.2% acceptance | 31.1 t/s |
| decode, cold first request | 28.1-30.4 t/s | (cold reads 20-55% low) |
| prefill @ ~4.4K depth, lazy SSD | **277.6-283.6 t/s** (4 runs, 2 sessions) | 395.6 t/s (IQ3 @4K; IQ4 llama-bench pp4096: 501.6 warm) |
| plain decode tail after prefill | 21.3-25.1 t/s | ~19-21 t/s @16-20K |

**llama-bench pair (2026-09-03, BENCHMARKS.md methodology, same flags):**

| test | Windows | Linux (IQ4_XS, warm cache) |
|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 | 314.05 +/- 52.35 | 501.6 |
| tg128 @ d0 | **22.77 +/- 0.18** | 22.8 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 258.79 +/- 2.56 | 379.3 |
| tg128 @ d16384 | **19.44 +/- 0.18** | 20.1 |

Reading: decode matches Linux to within noise at both depths - the
bandwidth-bound path is at full parity (same LPDDR5X). Prefill sits at 63-68%
of Linux even in llama-bench, i.e. **the gap is in the compute path, not in
the server or the SSD-lazy machinery** (earlier suspicion of
`PrefetchVirtualMemory`/page-cache effects is largely ruled out for this
metric). WDDM launch overhead is also a poor fit - decode issues far more
kernel launches per token and shows no gap. The pattern
(compute-throughput-bound path slow, bandwidth-bound path at parity) points
at sustained GPU compute clocks / power limits: the Linux box ran the TuneD
`accelerator-performance` profile, while this Windows box measured on the
default Balanced power plan.

**Elimination series (2026-09-03, all on the same llama-bench command):**

| variable toggled | pp4096 @ d0 | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Windows power slider Balanced -> Best Performance | 314 -> 308 (noise) | no effect |
| EVO-X2 front-panel P-mode -> Performance (red) | -> 322 (noise) | no effect - prefill is not power-limited here |
| `ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT` on vs off, warm pages | **350.8** vs 341.3 (+/-0.5) | engaged and worth +2.8% - not the gap |
| BIOS Main -> Power Mode Select: Balance -> Performance | 345.2 warm, 258.9 @16K | no effect (16K identical to +/-0.01) |

The warm-state pp4096 @ d0 is 350.8 t/s (the mixed cold/warm runs above read
lower because the first rep pays cold engram reads - +/-50 variance), so the
honest warm-vs-warm ratio against Linux's 501.6 is 70%. With SSD-lazy,
server, and hipBLASLt all eliminated, decode at exact parity, and all three
power levers (Windows slider, front-panel P-mode, BIOS Power Mode Select)
proven no-ops, the last two suspects were the driver's compute clock policy
and device codegen. HWiNFO telemetry settled it: **during llama-bench
prefill the GPU sustains ~2.8 GHz (max ~2.9) while delivering ~339 t/s** -
the clock is fine, so the kernels are doing less work per clock than the
Linux build. Power telemetry agrees: APU STAPM sits at ~34% of its limit
(~40-50 W) during prefill - the chip is nowhere near a power wall, so
power-unlock tools (RyzenAdj etc.) have nothing to unlock here. (An earlier 1.6-1.8 GHz reading was taken under mixed
server/decode load, where low clocks are normal DVFS and harmless.)
A ubatch sweep (2048/4096/8192) moved nothing: warm pp4096 stays in the
340-360 band at every size.

### Toolchain A/B: building against ROCm 7.14 on Windows, step by step

Goal: rebuild the identical tree against the same ROCm generation the Linux
container uses (7.14) to test whether the newer toolchain caused the prefill
gap. Getting 7.14 onto Windows has some traps; the full path taken on
2026-09-04:

**1. Finding a 7.14 distribution.** The stable pip index
(`stable.repo.amd.com/rocm/whl-next/`) carries exactly one version (10.0.0),
and TheRock's RELEASES.md states that 7.14 nightlies live only on the legacy
per-family index. Versions there are listed by
`pip index versions rocm --index-url https://rocm.nightlies.amd.com/v2/gfx1151/`;
the last 7.14 build is `7.14.0a20260612`.

**2. The pip route is broken - do not use it.** Installing
`rocm[libraries,devel]==7.14.0a20260612` from that index succeeds, but the
7.14-era devel wheel needs a manual `rocm-sdk init`, and on Windows that
expands 4.5 GB of *test binaries* into `_rocm_sdk_devel\bin` with empty
`include/`, `lib/`, and `cmake/` directories - no headers, no
`hip-config.cmake`, nothing to build against. (The 10.0.0 stable devel wheel
is fine; only the legacy nightly one is broken.)

**3. Use the TheRock tarball instead** (the same source lemonade's builds
use). Naming pattern `therock-dist-windows-<gfx>-<version>.tar.gz`;
availability can be probed with a HEAD request:

```powershell
curl.exe -sI https://therock-nightly-tarball.s3.amazonaws.com/therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0a20260612.tar.gz
# HTTP 200, ~2.5 GB
curl.exe -sL -o therock-714.tar.gz https://therock-nightly-tarball.s3.amazonaws.com/therock-dist-windows-gfx1151-7.14.0a20260612.tar.gz
mkdir C:\opt\rocm714
tar -xzf therock-714.tar.gz -C C:\opt\rocm714
```

The tarball has the classic layout: `lib\cmake\` with all package configs,
`lib\llvm\bin\` with clang/clang++, runtime DLLs in `bin\`.

**4. Configure and build** - same recipe as the main build, only the paths
and a separate build directory change:

```powershell
& "C:\...\Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
$rocm = "C:\opt\rocm714"
$env:PATH = "$rocm\lib\llvm\bin;$rocm\bin;<ninja dir>;$env:PATH"
cmake -S . -B build-rocm714 -G Ninja `
  -DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 `
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ `
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
  "-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$rocm\lib\cmake;$rocm" `
  -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build-rocm714 --target llama-bench   # ~15 min
```

**5. Run with the matching runtime.** The 7.14 binaries must load 7.14 DLLs -
put `C:\opt\rocm714\bin` first on PATH (not the 10.0 wheel directories):

```powershell
$env:PATH = "C:\opt\rocm714\bin;$env:PATH"
$env:ROCBLAS_USE_HIPBLASLT = "1"
# warm-up pass first (cold engram reads distort rep 1), then the measured pass:
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 16 -r 2
.\build-rocm714\bin\llama-bench.exe -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 `
  -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub 2048 -t 4 -p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2
```

**Result** (vs the 10.0-wheel build of the same tree, same day, same flags):

| | 7.14 tarball build | 10.0 wheel build |
|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 (warm rep) | ~345 | ~345-351 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | 260.15 +/- 0.80 | 258.9 |
| tg128 / @16K | 22.33 / 19.10 | 22.7 / 19.4 |

Identical within noise - **the toolchain is exonerated**. Both SDKs ship
"AMD clang 23.0.0git", just different llvm-project snapshots (`52226beb` in
7.14 vs `8f497e09` in 10.0), and neither is the cause.
`GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1` on the same build also changes nothing
(tg128 22.56 vs 22.3), so per-launch WDDM submission overhead is not the
story either.

**Final verdict (clock telemetry closed it):** correlated HWiNFO readings
show the two regimes directly - during heavy compute phases power rises to
~45 W and the GFX clock sits at **~1.8 GHz**, while the 2.6-2.8 GHz readings
occur in light phases at *lower* power. The GPU runs its GEMMs at ~1.8 GHz
by DVFS policy despite ~3x STAPM headroom: 1.8/2.9 = 62% of max clock,
which (plus small factors) accounts for the entire 69% prefill ratio.
The Linux reference pins this away - TuneD `accelerator-performance` forces
the amdgpu performance level high - while Adrenalin exposes no equivalent
control for the iGPU. So: not a bug in this branch, not the toolchain, not
power limits - a Windows driver DVFS policy for sustained compute, with no
known userspace override as of this writing. Decode, being bandwidth-bound,
is indifferent to it. Accept 70% prefill / 100% decode on Windows, or watch
Adrenalin releases for a compute/performance-level control.

### Real-workload statistics (Claude Code session, same day)

Aggregated from the server's `print_timing` lines over one evening of actual
Claude Code use against this server - 49 completed requests, conversation
depth growing past 50K tokens. Not a benchmark: mixed request sizes, mixed
content, one continuous session.

| | weighted average | per-request range |
|---|---|---|
| prefill | 196.7 t/s (131,429 tokens / 668 s) | 37.9 - 226.7 t/s |
| decode | 17.4 t/s (30,669 tokens / 1,760 s) | 12.4 - 26.3 t/s |
| MTP draft acceptance | 66.4% (19,821 / 29,854) | 40.0% - 92.3% |

Reading the numbers:

* The server-side prompt cache works: the full 50,623-token prefill happened
  once (cold start after a server restart, 223 s); every later turn prefilled
  only its delta (tens to a few thousand tokens). Per-turn wait is a few
  seconds to ~20 s of prefill plus generation.
* Decode below the 30 t/s short-context figure is the depth curve, not a
  Windows problem - at 50K+ depth the Linux reference is ~21 t/s MTP / ~13
  plain, which is exactly where these requests sit.
* Acceptance 66% average matches the Linux deep-context measurements (73.5%
  at 78K, 66% at 156K); the 40-56% outliers are free-form reasoning, the
  80-92% ones code.
* Low prefill t/s on tiny deltas (38 tokens at 37.9 t/s) is fixed overhead,
  under a second of absolute time.

Practical lever: keep working depth under ~30K (`/compact` early, fresh
sessions per task) and decode stays in the 20-25 t/s band.

Not measured on Windows: depth curves past 4.4K under controlled conditions,
llama-bench, PPL, multi-slot, RAM mode, the GDN chunk kernel
(`GGML_HIP_GDN_CHUNK=1`), and `test-qsa-gather-ms` (needs `--model`, not yet
run against the downloaded shards).

## Expert-pruned GSQ-RCO Coder vs IQ4_XS (2026-10-01)

[ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-Coder-GGUF)
is the same architecture with 256 of the 512 routed experts removed per layer
(RCO expert pruning) and the remaining weights at ~3.5 bpw (GSQ). The release
is code/agentic/vision targeted; the model card reports 91% of the base
SWE-bench Verified score and 99% of LiveCodeBench. Two shards, 58.4 GB total:
29.6 GB transformer (must be resident) + 28.8 GB engram table (IQ4_NL, same
lazy SSD path as the unsloth quants) + a 0.9 GB BF16 mmproj.

**Compatibility, checked before running:** `general.architecture = qwen4exp`,
`expert_count = 256`, `expert_used_count = 10`, and every hyper_connection /
ple / indexer / compress_ratios key this branch's loader reads is present. The
expert count comes from the metadata; nothing in the branch assumes 512. The
`IQ1_M` in the file name is a label only - the tensors are IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS /
IQ3_S / IQ4_NL / IQ4_XS / Q2_0 / Q4_K / Q5_K / Q6_K / Q8_0 / BF16 (per-tensor
map in `tensor-allocation/*.rco-allocation.txt`), all of which the HIP backend
has mmq / mmvq / getrows / convert kernels for. One difference from unsloth:
the router (`ffn_gate_inp`), `hc_*`, `ssm_alpha/beta` and `ple_key/value`
tensors are BF16 instead of F32 / Q8_0. It loads and runs on the build above
with no source change; the vision modality is reported on with the BF16
mmproj. Download note: this box has a wired default route; to pull over Wi-Fi
only, bind curl to the WLAN address (`curl.exe --interface <wlan-ip> -L -C -`).

**Procedure:** both models measured back to back on the same day, same
binary, same flags as the tables above, nothing else on the GPU. llama-bench:
one warm-up pass (`-p 4096 -n 16 -r 2`) then the measured pass
(`-p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2`). Server: `-c 163840`, q8_0 KV, `-lm mmap
-lzm on`, hipBLASLt on, the EasiiX MTP sidecar + `draft-mtp,ngram-mod` on both
(the sidecar is a separate draft model and does not depend on the target's
expert count), temperature 0, 400 tokens out, numbers from the `timings`
object. Request order per server: a short real-code prompt as cold first
request, a fresh short real-code prompt (measured decode), a ~4.75K-token
chunk of `llama-model-loader.cpp` (measured prefill + decode tail), then the
first prompt repeated (reference only - prompt cache and ngram have seen it).

**llama-bench pair:**

| test | GSQ-RCO Coder | IQ4_XS, same day | IQ4_XS, 2026-09-03 above |
|---|---|---|---|
| pp4096 @ d0 | 318.1 +/- 70.0 (warm-up pass: 365.3) | 339.5 +/- 6.0 (warm-up pass: 337.2) | 314.1 +/- 52.4 (warm 350.8) |
| tg128 @ d0 | 20.92 +/- 0.19 | 21.83 +/- 0.52 | 22.77 +/- 0.18 |
| pp4096 @ d16384 | **269.9 +/- 1.2** | 244.1 +/- 19.5 | 258.8 +/- 2.6 |
| tg128 @ d16384 | 17.98 +/- 0.15 | 16.25 +/- 4.23 | 19.44 +/- 0.18 |

The IQ4_XS d16384 rows were noisy this day (+/-4 on tg128, below the
September numbers); treat the September column as the better IQ4_XS anchor
for those two cells. The +/-70 on the GSQ d0 prefill is the usual cold first
rep (engram reads), same as documented above.

**Server timings:**

| | GSQ-RCO Coder | IQ4_XS, same day | IQ4_XS, 2026-09-02 above |
|---|---|---|---|
| model load to listening | **30 s** | 83 s | 1m28s-1m34s |
| cold first request, decode (MTP) | 26.1 t/s, 86.5% acc | 28.2 t/s, 87.8% acc | 28.1-30.4 t/s |
| fresh code prompt, decode (MTP) | 21.9 t/s, 74.5% acc | 25.1 t/s, 78.2% acc | 30.1-30.7 t/s, 89.2% acc |
| prefill @ 4754 depth | **321.5 t/s** | 277.2 t/s | 277.6-283.6 t/s |
| decode tail after that prefill | 20.8 t/s, 81.9% acc | 23.0 t/s, 84.9% acc | 21.3-25.1 t/s |
| repeated prompt (reference only) | 49.9 t/s | 58.6 t/s, 99.2% acc | |

**Reading the numbers:**

* Pruning does not speed up decode. Decode is bandwidth-bound on the 10
  active experts per token, and that count is unchanged; the retained weights
  use IQ2_S / IQ3_XXS / Q2_0 types whose dequant costs more per byte than
  IQ4_XS, so decode lands ~5-10% below IQ4_XS at every depth.
* Prefill at depth is where the halved expert count shows: a batch touches
  every expert of a layer, so expert weight traffic halves and pp4096 @ 16K
  is +4% (vs the September anchor) to +10% (same day), the 4.75K server
  prefill +16%.
* Load time drops from ~85 s to 30 s and the on-disk footprint from 87 GiB to
  54 GiB (GPU-resident part ~30 GB vs 60 GB), which is the practical win: it
  fits a 64 GB carve with room for context.
* The fresh-prompt acceptance (74-78%) is lower than the September 89% on both
  models for a prompt reason, not a model one: the "fresh" prompt pasted a
  type-trait table instead of a function, both models correctly refused to
  rewrite it and answered in prose, and prose drafts worse than code. The
  comparison between the two models holds; the absolute number is not the
  code-decode figure of the earlier tables.
* No quality comparison yet: on the 4.75K prompt both models spent the whole
  400-token budget in reasoning, and the two short prompts were answered
  correctly by both. Quality vs IQ4_XS on real agent work is unmeasured.

1:# Benchmarks & methodology — Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next on Strix Halo
38:## Methodology
43:  `POST /completion` with `"temperature": 0`, numbers from the `timings` object.
44:  Code prompt = rewrite-a-function task (400 tokens out), prose prompt =
46:* **Depth curves** in one pass: one server, one slot, the prompt grows as a
47:  strict prefix (`cache_prompt: true`), so each stage prefills only its delta.
61:  `-lm none` load). Do a warm-up request first.
63:  ~35% fast (prompt cache + the ngram speculator has seen the answer: 52.7 vs
64:  39.3 t/s in our tests). Always use a fresh prompt for the measured run.
65:* **Synthetic prompts break MTP decode numbers:** after a random-word filler
66:  prompt at temperature 0 the model degenerates into repetitive output, the
69:  prefill (pp) is unaffected by prompt content.
180:**MTP decode at depth (server, real code payloads, temperature 0, Q8_0
190:per-step attention/indexer cost. A 156K-token prompt prefills in ~12 minutes
191:(221.7 t/s average over the whole prompt with the sidecar loaded) and then
194:Prefill with the full MTP stack loaded (server, `cache_prompt=false`, fresh
195:~4–86K-token prompts): 464 t/s avg at 5.4K, 402 at 21K, 342 at 43K, 272 at
225:Server, 32K slot, temperature 0, IQ3 target. Rows 1–4 were measured on the

## Methodology

* **llama-bench** for flag/quant comparisons:
  `llama-bench -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub <n> -t <n> -p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2 -o json`
* **Server timings** for speculation and end-to-end configs: `llama-server` +
  `POST /completion` with `"temperature": 0`, numbers from the `timings` object.
  Code prompt = rewrite-a-function task (400 tokens out), prose prompt =
  descriptive text (300 tokens out, `ignore_eos`).
* **Depth curves** in one pass: one server, one slot, the prompt grows as a
  strict prefix (`cache_prompt: true`), so each stage prefills only its delta.
  pp = delta rate, decode = 64 tokens at that depth. Deepest stage: 236,730
  real tokens.
* **Exclusive box:** all other GPU/RAM services stopped during measurement.
  Never overlap container builds with measurements (we lost a run to the OOM
  killer that way).
* One variable per run, against a named anchor.
* The chunked GDN prefill kernel is opt-in on RDNA3/RDNA4 via
  `GGML_HIP_GDN_CHUNK=1` and was **not** enabled in any run below.

### Measurement pitfalls (you will hit these)

* **Cold-start reads low:** the first request after server/model load measures
  20–55% slow (worst case observed: 17.8 vs 39.3 t/s right after a full
  `-lm none` load). Do a warm-up request first.
* **Repeats read high:** sending the identical request again measures up to
  ~35% fast (prompt cache + the ngram speculator has seen the answer: 52.7 vs
  39.3 t/s in our tests). Always use a fresh prompt for the measured run.
* **Synthetic prompts break MTP decode numbers:** after a random-word filler
  prompt at temperature 0 the model degenerates into repetitive output, the
  ngram speculator hits up to 100% draft acceptance, and decode reads 2–3x
  high (73 t/s observed). Measure MTP decode on real code/prose payloads only;
  prefill (pp) is unaffected by prompt content.
* PPL with 32K chunks OOMs on larger quants (logits buffer × 248,320 vocab ≈
  32 GiB fp32) — use 8K chunks.
* `llama-perplexity --multiple-choice` crashes on every build of the qwen4exp

## Methodology

* **llama-bench** for flag/quant comparisons:
  `llama-bench -m <model> -ngl 999 -fa 1 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -lm mmap -b 8192 -ub <n> -t <n> -p 4096 -n 128 -d 0,16384 -r 2 -o json`
* **Server timings** for speculation and end-to-end configs: `llama-server` +
  `POST /completion` with `"temperature": 0`, numbers from the `timings` object.
  Code prompt = rewrite-a-function task (400 tokens out), prose prompt =
  descriptive text (300 tokens out, `ignore_eos`).
* **Depth curves** in one pass: one server, one slot, the prompt grows as a
  strict prefix (`cache_prompt: true`), so each stage prefills only its delta.
  pp = delta rate, decode = 64 tokens at that depth. Deepest stage: 236,730
  real tokens.
* **Exclusive box:** all other GPU/RAM services stopped during measurement.
  Never overlap container builds with measurements (we lost a run to the OOM
  killer that way).
* One variable per run, against a named anchor.
* The chunked GDN prefill kernel is opt-in on RDNA3/RDNA4 via
  `GGML_HIP_GDN_CHUNK=1` and was **not** enabled in any run below.

### Measurement pitfalls (you will hit these)

* **Cold-start reads low:** the first request after server/model load measures
  20–55% slow (worst case observed: 17.8 vs 39.3 t/s right after a full
  `-lm none` load). Do a warm-up request first.
* **Repeats read high:** sending the identical request again measures up to
  ~35% fast (prompt cache + the ngram speculator has seen the answer: 52.7 vs
  39.3 t/s in our tests). Always use a fresh prompt for the measured run.
* **Synthetic prompts break MTP decode numbers:** after a random-word filler
  prompt at temperature 0 the model degenerates into repetitive output, the
  ngram speculator hits up to 100% draft acceptance, and decode reads 2–3x
  high (73 t/s observed). Measure MTP decode on real code/prose payloads only;
  prefill (pp) is unaffected by prompt content.
* PPL with 32K chunks OOMs on larger quants (logits buffer × 248,320 vocab ≈
  32 GiB fp32) — use 8K chunks.
* `llama-perplexity --multiple-choice` crashes on every build of the qwen4exp
