lines: -# A manual install into a conda environment (RTX 3060 Laptop, the Coder IQ1_M)
+# Strata on an RTX 3060 Laptop: a manual conda install, speed and BFCL against llama.cpp
-This page records an install done by hand, without `setup.py`: the same steps setup does, with every dependency in
-an active conda environment (`strata`) instead of `.venv` and a system CUDA toolkit. Use it when you want Strata in
-your own conda environment, have no sudo, or already have the GGUF files.
+This page records work on one laptop (RTX 3060 Laptop 12 GB, Ryzen 9 8945HX, 92 GB RAM), 2026-10-02/03:
+- an install done by hand, without `setup.py`: the same steps setup does, with every dependency in an active conda
+  environment (`strata`) instead of `.venv` and a system CUDA toolkit. Use it when you want Strata in your own conda
+  environment, have no sudo, or already have the GGUF files;
+- the GSQ-RCO Coder IQ1_M and Unsloth's UD-IQ4_XS (not a setup choice) measured against llama.cpp on a Strix Halo,
+- `/v1/completions`, added to the server for BFCL's path B, and BFCL multi-turn pilots against the Strix Halo's
+- where the CPU time goes during BFCL (threads, SMT, temperatures).
other in decode (windows.md): there the model's size costs memory, here it costs GPU expert-cache room.
- The repeated prompt is again where llama.cpp leads (58.6 vs 42.6 t/s): its ngram speculator drafts the answer it
+BFCL's path B renders the Qwen3 prompt itself and sends it to `/v1/completions`, which Strata did not have. It was
+- the prompt is one string (special tokens such as `<|im_start|>` read as tokens, as llama.cpp does) or one list of
+- the model's text comes back unparsed: `<think>` and `<tool_call>` stay in `text` (a pass-through parser in place
+  of `OutputParser`; the queue, timings, history and engine restarts are the chat endpoint's);
+- `stop` (a string or a list) ends the text before the first match; a stream holds back text that may be the start
+  of one; `max_tokens` unset / 0 / -1 = the rest of the context, a prompt that does not fit is a 400;
+- OpenAI's `text_completion` shape, streamed or not, with `usage` (`cached_tokens`) and llama.cpp's `timings`;
+On the engine (Coder IQ1_M): a raw Qwen prompt answered with `timings` (36.2 t/s, 15/15 drafts accepted); `stop:
+["return"]` cut the text right before it; a prompt ending at `assistant\n` returned the model's own
+`<think>...</think>` as text; the next request reused 17 cached prompt tokens.
+## BFCL multi-turn against llama.cpp on the Strix Halo
+The Strix Halo runs are in freetoken (`README.md`, "BFCL multi-turn 测试计划"; runs in `bfcl/runs/`): llama.cpp HIP
+on the Radeon 8060S, the same two model files, BFCL at gorilla `6ea5797` with local handlers, temperature 0.001,
+one request at a time. Two paths:
+- **A, native function calling** (what Claude Code uses): `/v1/chat/completions` + `tools`. The server's chat
+  template and tool parser are part of what is measured; llama.cpp used the froggeric v22.5 template, Strata the
+- **B, BFCL's own prompt**: BFCL renders the Qwen3 prompt and parses `<tool_call>` itself, through
+  `/v1/completions`. The prompt is the same text for both engines: only the weights and the engine are measured.
+- `setup-bfcl.sh`: a conda environment `bfcl-py312` (BFCL's dependencies stay out of `strata`), gorilla at
+  `6ea5797` with the Windows checkout's handler changes applied, `bfcl-eval` editable, and a Qwen3.8 tokenizer for
+  path B (only the small files of the Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 folder the Windows runs used: BFCL counts the prompt's
+  tokens with it and reads the context length, 262144, from its `config.json`).
+  generate + evaluate into `~/work/AI/bfcl/runs/<config>-<path>-<think>-<cat>-<stamp>/` with the same `run.json`
+  keys as the Windows `run-bfcl.ps1`, so its `summarize-bfcl.py` reads both. `--start` starts the Strata server for
+  the config and stops it at the end; `--resume` continues a stopped run in its own folder (entries that ended in an
+  inference error are removed first - BFCL keeps them and scores them 0 - then BFCL generates only the missing ids).
+**The 32K context.** BFCL asks for `min(4096, 262144 - prompt)` = 4096 new tokens. Base and miss_param prompts
+peaked at 14.7K tokens on the Halo, so they fit in this config's 32K; two of the pilot's long_context items
+(`multi_turn_long_context_100` and `_120`, prompts of 35.2K-35.6K tokens) do not, and Strata refuses them with a
+400 (requests are never truncated). They count as wrong in every Strata pilot below; the Halo served 163K.
+The pilot is 10 items of each category (`pilot_ids.json`: ids 0, 20, ... 180).
+| model | engine | path | overall | base | miss_func | miss_param | long_ctx | out tok/call |
+(Wilson 95% intervals; transport errors 0 in every run.) The Halo has no GSQ pilot: for the GSQ rows below, its
+400-item runs are scored on the pilot's 20 base + miss_param ids.
+**Same 20 ids (base + miss_param), and time per call** (BFCL's own latency per model call; the Halo's numbers from
+| model | engine, path | right | model time | s/call | tok/call |
+Per call this PC with Strata is 1.4-1.7x faster than the Halo with llama.cpp at about the same output length per
+call (engine and hardware together, as above). BFCL calls are mostly prompt: 14-27K characters in, 50-90 tokens
+### The UD-IQ4_XS gap on path B
+With the GSQ Coder the two engines score the same on path B (11 vs 10 of 20). With UD-IQ4_XS Strata scores lower:
+45.0 vs 67.5 on the 40 pilot items. Item by item (path B pilots):
+- both right 18, both wrong 13, only llama.cpp right 9, only Strata right 0 (exact McNemar p = 0.004 against this
+  one llama.cpp run). Two of the 9 are the over-length items Strata refuses at 32K.
+- The prompts are byte-identical (checked on 5 items, 14-27K characters each, ending in BFCL's empty think block).
+- In 6 of the other 7 the answers differ from the first generated text, often from the first word.
+- **llama.cpp does not agree with itself either.** Its pilot and its 400-item run, the same 20 base + miss_param
+  ids: first step identical 8/20, whole item identical 2/20; llama.cpp against Strata: first step identical
+  4-6/20, whole item 0/20. Its two runs scored 13 and 12 of those 20, Strata 9.
+So the first-step divergence alone proves nothing (temperature 0.001 and speculative decoding make runs differ),
+but the score gap is larger than llama.cpp's own run-to-run spread. What differs from the GSQ Coder, where the
+engines match: UD-IQ4_XS is prepared by hand with `--compat-bf16`, which rounds 195 tensors (1.20 GiB) to BF16
+(largest absolute error 0.0144); the GSQ pack needs no conversion. That is the first suspect; it is not tested.
+**The 400-item path B run** on UD-IQ4_XS (base + miss_param, thinking off) is running to settle this against
+llama.cpp's 400-item path B (base 59.0, miss_param 37.5; about +-5 points at 400 items): 50 of 400 after 26 min,
+29.6 s per item. Its result goes here when it ends.
+## Where the CPU time goes during BFCL
+The Ryzen 9 8945HX has 16 cores on two chiplets (CCD1: cores 0-7, CCD2: 8-15) and 32 threads: logical CPUs 16-31
+are the SMT siblings of cores 0-15 (`lscpu -e`). The engine pins one expert-pool worker per physical core (15
+workers on cores 1-15, `src/kernels/cpu/pool.cpp`) and its host thread on core 0, which spins to answer the GPU
+without delay; the SMT siblings are left idle on purpose (`src/core/session.cpp`: another thread on a worker's core
+or its sibling took the CPU path from 36.3 to 26.9 GB/s on the machine that was measured).
+Measured over 5 s during the 400-item UD-IQ4_XS path B run (`/proc/stat`):
+| | core 0 | cores 1-15 (expert workers) | SMT siblings 16-31 | clock |
+The GPU was at 100%. The workers are idle most of the time because a BFCL call is mostly prompt, and Strata reads
+prompts on the GPU; the expert pool only works during the short decode. More threads (the 16 SMT siblings,
+`--pool-workers 31`) would add workers to a pool that waits most of the time, and the CPU's expert path is limited by
+memory bandwidth, which a sibling does not add. For long answers (decode-heavy work such as coding sessions) the
+worker count can matter; `tools/calibrate.py` tries fewer workers than the default. Not measured on this PC.
+Temperatures at the same time (`~/temp.sh`): CPU Tccd1 87.1 °C, Tccd2 63.1 °C, Tctl 85.0 °C; GPU 60 °C at 100%;
+iGPU 57 °C; SSD 42.8 °C. CCD1 is warmer because it holds core 0 with the spinning host thread (and seven other
+engine threads pinned to CPU 0), and it runs about 180 MHz faster than CCD2; the worker load is spread evenly over

results.content:
correctly by both. Quality vs IQ4_XS on real agent work is unmeasured.

**BFCL multi-turn, GSQ-RCO Coder vs IQ4_XS (2026-10-01 to 10-03):** the
tool-calling quality comparison that the tables above lacked. Protocol and
harness are the ones in `E:\work\AI\freetoken\README.md` ("BFCL multi-turn"):
Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v4 multi-turn, `multi_turn_base` +
`multi_turn_miss_param` (200 entries each), temperature 0.001, this
llama-server with the MTP sidecar, path A = native `/v1/chat/completions`
tool calls through the server's template and parser (what Claude Code uses),
path B = BFCL's own Qwen3 text protocol over `/v1/completions` (weights
only). Thinking on/off is the template's `enable_thinking`. Transport errors
were 0 in all runs. 400 entries give a Wilson 95% interval of about +/-5,
200-entry subcategories about +/-7.

| path / thinking | GSQ-RCO Coder | IQ4_XS | base GSQ / IQ4 | miss_param GSQ / IQ4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A native FC, off | 48.5 | 48.2 | **64.5** / 57.0 | 32.5 / 39.5 |
| B text protocol, off | 53.2 | 48.2 | **69.0** / 59.0 | 37.5 / 37.5 |
| A native FC, on | **60.2** | 57.0 | **79.0** / 67.0 | 41.5 / 47.0 |
| B text protocol, on | 55.2 | 50.8 | **69.5** / 59.5 | 41.0 / 42.0 |

| path / thinking | s/entry GSQ / IQ4 | calls/entry GSQ / IQ4 | out tok/call GSQ / IQ4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| A off | **55** / 62 | 14.1 / 13.4 | 59 / 72 |
| B off | **50** / 52 | 13.0 / 11.5 | 51 / 61 |
| A on | 97 / 95 | 12.4 / 12.0 | 160 / 150 |
| B on | 121 / 120 | 12.2 / 12.0 | 144 / 145 |

* Same shape in all four runs: base +7.5 to +12 (the +10 and +12 cells do
  not overlap IQ4_XS's interval), miss_param equal to -7. That is what a
  code/agentic-targeted pruning should look like: plain tool calling
  improves, knowing when to stop and ask for a missing parameter does not.
* With thinking off the pruned model overruns the 20-step limit 5x more
  often on path A (56 vs 11 entries): it keeps calling rather than stopping.
  Thinking on brings that to 7 and lifts miss_param from 32.5 to 41.5.
* On the Claude Code path with thinking on, 60.2 vs 57.0, inside the band of
  the 27B models on the same two subcategories (61-63), at half the resident
  VRAM. miss_param stays 5.5 below IQ4_XS: it is more likely to call with a
  guessed parameter than to ask.
* Speed: thinking off 4-11% less wall time per entry (faster prefill,
  shorter outputs); thinking on equal (longer reasoning on miss_param eats
  the prefill gain). Single pass each; the noise floor measured for
  llama.cpp single-slot + MTP on the 27B runs was <= 0.5 points.

Where the BFCL data lives (all under `E:\work\AI\freetoken\bfcl\runs\`, one
directory per run, 216-260 MB each; the GSQ runs are
`gsq-hip-<A|B>-<off|on>-...-gsq-r1` and `...-gsq-think1`):

* `result\<handler>\multi_turn\BFCL_v4_multi_turn_<base|miss_param>_result.json`:
  one JSON line per test entry with `id`, `result` (the function calls the
  model issued, per turn), `input_token_count`, `output_token_count`,
  `latency` (nested per turn and per call), and `inference_log` (the full
  round trip, since the runs used `--include-input-log`: every message sent
  to the model, the raw reply including reasoning and tool calls, the tool
  results and the backend state snapshots). To see why an entry failed, read
  its line here.
* `score\<handler>\multi_turn\BFCL_v4_multi_turn_<cat>_score.json`: first
  line is the accuracy, every following line is one failed entry with the
  error type and the diff against the ground truth. `score\*.csv` are the
  leaderboard-format summaries.
* `run.json` (config, path, handler, endpoint, BFCL commit, start time),
  `generate.log` / `evaluate.log` (UTF-16, read with PowerShell
  `Get-Content`, not grep), and `resume.log` on the run that was paused.
* Outside the run directories: `runs\summary-gsq.md` (the summary table),
  `bfcl\server-flashnext-gsq-r1.err.log` and `...-gsq-think1.err.log`
  (llama-server side, `print_timing` and draft acceptance per request).
* The few generations from the speed tests earlier in this section were not
  archived; only their timings are recorded here.

Yes, they can be compared. The Halo now has 8 full runs: 2 models × paths A/B × thinking off/on, 400 items each. So far Strata has one matching 400-item run, UD-IQ4_XS path B with thinking off, and only its `multi_turn_base` half is finished.

**Matched comparison so far:** UD-IQ4_XS, path B, thinking off, the same 200 `multi_turn_base` items.

| | Correct | Model time per item | Calls per item | Time per call | Tokens per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp, Strix Halo | 59.0% (118/200) | 49.4 s | 10.7 | 4.63 s | 61 |

steps.message:
The 400-item run finished, and it settles the question: on UD-IQ4_XS path B, Strata is as accurate as llama.cpp. On the same weights and the same prompts, Strata scored 52.2 against llama.cpp's 48.2.

**UD-IQ4_XS, path B, thinking off, the same 400 items:**

| | Overall | base | miss_param | Model time per item | Calls per item | Time per call | Tokens per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp, Strix Halo | 48.2 | 59.0 | 37.5 | 52.4 s | 11.5 | 4.55 s | 61 |
| Strata, RTX 3060 Laptop | **52.2** | **61.0** | **43.5** | **38.9 s** | 11.5 | 3.40 s | 61 |

- **Accuracy:** Strata's 4-point lead is within the noise of one run. Item by item, llama.cpp alone got 36 right and Strata alone got 52 (McNemar p = 0.11; base p = 0.64, miss_param p = 0.11). So the pilot's 9-to-0 was a small-sample effect, and the BF16 conversion (`--compat-bf16`) isn't hurting accuracy.
- **Speed:** the run took 4.3 h here against about 5.8 h on the Halo, 26% less model time per item. Calls and output tokens are the same, so the difference is in prompt reading and generation speed (engine and hardware together).
- **Errors:** 0 transport errors and 0 context refusals; all base and miss_param prompts fit in 32K. The failures are the usual model ones: 106 wrong final state, 51 empty turns, 31 wrong execution results, 3 step-limit hits.

I updated `docs/3060M.md`: the gap section now has the full 400-item table, the item-by-item tests and the timings, and calls the question settled. The raw results are in `~/work/AI/bfcl/runs/strata-iq4xs-B-off-…-r1/`, and the Strata server is stopped.

The other 7 cells of the Halo's matrix still have no full Strata run. The one that matters most for Claude Code is GSQ path A with thinking on, where the Halo scored 60.2; I'd estimate it at 6–8 hours, roughly twice the thinking-off time. Should I start it?

Before starting: the thinking handler asks for `max_tokens` 16384, and Strata refuses any prompt that leaves less room than that in 32K. I'll check the longest prompt the Halo saw in this exact run, and Strata's context slack:

steps.message:
Probably yes. The run is in a separate session from your SSH terminal (its own session id, no terminal), so a dropped connection doesn't signal it directly. But it is a background task of this Claude Code process (`claude`, pid 15104, on `pts/0`), and Claude Code isn't running inside tmux or screen. When SSH drops, Claude Code gets a hangup and exits, and it normally cleans up the background tasks it started. That would stop BFCL, and then the run script's exit trap stops the server.

If that happens, nothing is lost except the item in progress. `tools/bfcl/run-bfcl.sh --resume <run folder> --start` continues from the last finished item.

To make it independent of the SSH session now, I can stop this run and restart it with `--resume` under `setsid nohup`, fully detached from Claude Code and the terminal. That loses only the item currently running. The downside: I would no longer get a notification when it ends, so you would check its log or `run.json`. For future long runs, starting Claude Code inside `tmux` keeps everything alive across disconnects.

Should I restart it detached?

I've restarted the run fully detached, so closing SSH or Claude Code no longer stops it. The 6 finished items were kept, and only the item that was running then is redone.

- **Stopping the old run took two tries.** My first `pgrep` also matched its own shell and killed that command partway. I then stopped the run script, BFCL and the server by PID. The run was never scored and its 6 saved items are intact.
- **The new process** runs with `setsid nohup` and stdin closed. Its parent is PID 1, it has its own session and no terminal, so neither SSH nor Claude Code is its parent any more.
- **Checking on it later.** I won't get a notification when it ends. Its console output is in the run folder:
  ```bash
  R=~/work/AI/bfcl/runs/strata-gsq-A-on-multi_turn_base+multi_turn_miss_param-20261003-2032-think1
  tail -c 300 $R/detached.log          # progress (x/394)
  ls $R/score                          # exists once it has finished and been scored
  ```
- **To stop it** (it would continue with `--resume` later):
  ```bash
  pkill -f "run-bfcl.sh --resume"
  ```

steps.message:
The run is healthy: 18 items done, at about 58 s per item, so about 6 hours remain. It runs independently of this session, and the server reloaded in 11 s.

**Why 397 rather than 394:** `--resume` kept 3 of the 6 saved items and removed 3 that had ended in errors, as designed. Those 3 were broken by my first stop attempt, the one that killed only the outer wrapper and its own shell:
- `multi_turn_base_4` and `_5`: "Connection error", sent while the server was going down.
- `multi_turn_base_3`: the server answered `400 'I/O operation on closed file.'`

That last error points to a small robustness issue in Strata. When the outer wrapper died, the server's standard output closed. Its next progress `print` raised a `ValueError`, and the request handler turns `ValueError` into a 400 "invalid request". So with stdout gone, every request would fail as if the client had sent a bad request. The detached run sends output to a file, so it can't happen here. It's worth a fix in `serve/server.py` (ignore failed progress prints) if you want one.

My 15-minute monitor reported nothing only because it waited for "/394". Progress can be checked with:
```bash
tail -c 300 ~/work/AI/bfcl/runs/strata-gsq-A-on-multi_turn_base+multi_turn_miss_param-20261003-2032-think1/detached.log
```

arguments.command:
cd /home/luwei/work/AI/Strata; python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p = "docs/3060M.md"; t = open(p).read()
s = t.index("## The PC\n"); e = t.index("## Why not setup.py")
new = '''## The PC

A desktop mini board, not a laptop: a mobile CPU (Ryzen 9 8945HX) on a mini-ITX-class board, and a mobile GPU chip
(GA106M, "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU") on a desktop PCIe card, the kind sold as a converted laptop GPU (subsystem ID
`10de:0000`, no OEM's). The model's experts live in system RAM; the GPU holds the dense layers, the KV cache and a
cache of experts (2666 of the Coder's, 1864 of UD-IQ4_XS's); the experts it does not hold are computed by the CPU
from RAM or copied to the GPU over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). So the numbers that matter are the GPU's VRAM and memory
bandwidth, the PCIe link, the RAM's bandwidth and the CPU's cores. Read on 2026-10-03 with `lscpu`, `nvidia-smi -q`,
sysfs and `lspci`; "spec" marks a vendor figure, "measured" one measured on this PC.

**GPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| Card | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Laptop GPU, GA106M (`10de:2520`, rev a1), Ampere, compute capability 8.6; VBIOS 94.06.0F.00.AE |
| VRAM | 12288 MiB GDDR6; memory clock 7001 MHz (14 Gbps effective); 192-bit bus, 336 GB/s (spec for GA106 at 14 Gbps) |
| Cores, clocks | 30 SMs, 3840 CUDA cores (spec); graphics clock up to 2100 MHz, 1980 MHz seen under the BFCL load |
| Power | 80 W limit (default and current; the card allows 1-85 W); P0 under load; 60-64 °C at 100% load |
| PCIe link | **PCIe 4.0 x16** (16 GT/s, x16, the card's maximum; the slot can do 5.0): about 31.5 GB/s each way in theory |
| PCIe, measured | **26.8 GB/s host to device** (the engine's probe at every start, so `--pcie-frac 0.55`, the default) |
| BAR1 | 8192 MiB (less than the 12 GiB of VRAM) |
| Driver | 580.142, the official driver repacked by "FrankenDriver" for converted cards: same kernel module, plus `NVreg_RegistryDwords="RM1457588=1;"` (see `~/3060M-FrankenDriver-Linux.md`); GSP firmware on, persistence mode off, dynamic power management 3 |
| CUDA | 13.0 toolkit in the conda environment (nvcc 13.0.88, cuBLAS 13.1.1.3); the engine is built for sm_86 |

**CPU**

| | |
|---|---|
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 8945HX (Zen 4, mobile "HX"), 16 cores / 32 threads, 1 socket, 1 NUMA node |
| Layout | two chiplets: CCD1 = cores 0-7, CCD2 = cores 8-15; logical CPUs 16-31 are the SMT siblings of 0-15 |
| Caches | L1d 32 KiB + L1i 32 KiB per core, L2 1 MiB per core (16 MiB), L3 64 MiB (32 MiB per chiplet) |
| Vector | AVX2 and AVX-512 (F, BW, DQ, VL, CD, IFMA, VBMI, VBMI2, VNNI, **BF16**, BITALG, VPOPCNTDQ) |
| Clocks | 400-5461 MHz; measured under the BFCL load: 5083 MHz on CCD1, 4901 MHz on CCD2 |
| Power policy | `amd-pstate-epp`, governor `powersave`, energy preference `performance` |
| Strata's use | 15 expert-pool workers pinned to cores 1-15 and the host thread on core 0; SMT siblings left idle (see "Where the CPU time goes") |

**Memory**

| | |
|---|---|
| RAM | 98.8 GB seen by the OS (`free`), 92 GiB `MemTotal`; 2 GiB of it is the iGPU's carve-out (`mem_info_vram_total`) |
| Type, speed | **not read**: module type, speed and channel count need root (`sudo dmidecode -t memory`). The 8945HX supports dual-channel DDR5-5200 (spec): about 83 GB/s in theory |
| Measured | no RAM bandwidth test yet (it would disturb the BFCL run that was going). What the engine loads from the page cache: 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |
| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |

**Storage and network**

| | |
|---|---|
| SSD | Acer SSD N3500 1 TB (MAXIO MAP1202, DRAM-less), **PCIe 3.0 x4** (8 GT/s x4: about 3.9 GB/s in theory); root on LVM, 688 GB free |
| Measured | model load from the SSD: 2.6-2.9 GiB/s (55.4 GiB of UD-IQ4_XS experts in 20-21 s at 2.57-2.75 GiB/s; 23.4 GiB of Coder experts at 2.1 GiB/s), from the page cache 8.7-9.3 GiB/s |
| Network share | `/mnt/evox2` (SMB): 112 MB/s measured with `rsync` (59.3 GB in 8 min 24 s; 93.7 GB in 13 min 16 s); loading a model straight from it ran at 0.11 GiB/s |

**System and software**

| | |
|---|---|
| Board | "Micro Computer (HK) Tech Limited" / "Meigao Innovation Technology", product `MotherBoard Series`, board `DRFXL`, BIOS 1.14 (2025-11-13); chassis type 3 = desktop |
| iGPU | AMD Raphael (Radeon 610M class), PCIe-attached at 16 GT/s x16; not used by Strata |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Linux 6.8.0-136-generic, gcc 13.3.0 |
| Python | 3.14.7 in the conda environment `strata` (`~/miniconda3/envs/strata`); BFCL in `bfcl-py312` (Python 3.12) |
| Models | Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Coder IQ1_M (2 shards, 58.4 GB) and Unsloth UD-IQ4_XS (3 shards, 93.7 GB), in `~/Documents` |

'''
t = t[:s] + new + t[e:]
old = "This page records work on one laptop (RTX 3060 Laptop 12 GB, Ryzen 9 8945HX, 92 GB RAM), 2026-10-02/03:"
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, "This page records work on one desktop PC (RTX 3060 Laptop GPU 12 GB on a desktop card, Ryzen 9 8945HX, 92 GiB\nRAM; details in [The PC](#the-pc)), 2026-10-02/03:")
t = t.replace("# Strata on an RTX 3060 Laptop: a manual conda install", "# Strata on an RTX 3060 Laptop GPU: a manual conda install")
open(p, "w").write(t)
PYEOF
grep -n "^# \|desktop PC" docs/3060M.md | head -3; grep -n -iE "\blaptop\b" docs/3060M.md | grep -viE "3060 laptop" | head

steps.message:
I rewrote "The PC" section of `docs/3060M.md`. It now has tables for the GPU, CPU, memory, storage and network, and system and software, gathered with read-only queries so the BFCL run wasn't disturbed. The section opens by explaining which figures matter for inference: VRAM and GPU memory bandwidth, the PCIe link, RAM bandwidth and CPU cores.

**What's in it, by area:**
- **GPU:** GA106M "RTX 3060 Laptop GPU" on a desktop PCIe card.
  - VRAM: 12 GiB GDDR6 at 14 Gbps, 192-bit, 336 GB/s (spec).
  - Compute: 30 SMs, up to 2100 MHz; 80 W power limit.
  - **PCIe 4.0 x16**, the card's maximum (the slot supports 5.0), about 31.5 GB/s in theory. The engine measures **26.8 GB/s host to device** at every start.
  - BAR1 is 8 GiB.
  - Driver: the FrankenDriver repack of 580.142 with `RM1457588=1`.
- **CPU:** Ryzen 9 8945HX, 16 cores / 32 threads across two chiplets.
  - Cache: 64 MiB L3; AVX-512 including BF16 and VNNI.
  - Clocks: measured 5083 / 4901 MHz under load.
  - Power policy: `amd-pstate-epp` with the `performance` energy preference.
  - How Strata pins its threads.
- **Memory:** 92 GiB usable, 2 GiB of it reserved for the iGPU; THP `madvise`; 8 GiB swap file.
- **Storage:** Acer N3500 1 TB, a DRAM-less drive on **PCIe 3.0 x4**.
  - Measured model loads: 2.57–2.75 GiB/s for UD-IQ4_XS, 1.7–2.9 for the Coder, 8.7–9.3 GiB/s from the page cache.
  - The network share copies at 112 MB/s.
- **System:** Meigao / Minisforum-type board, BIOS 1.14, chassis type desktop; Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.8.0-136.

I also corrected the page's intro and title, which called this PC a laptop. It's a desktop with a converted laptop GPU, as your FrankenDriver notes show.

**Two gaps, both marked "not read" / "not measured" in the doc:**
- **RAM type, speed and channels** need root. If you run `! sudo dmidecode -t memory`, I'll fill them in. Until then the doc gives only the 8945HX's spec, dual-channel DDR5-5200 at about 83 GB/s.
- **Actual RAM bandwidth** hasn't been measured, since a test now would disturb the BFCL run. After the run ends I can measure it and the GPU's device-to-host speed in a few minutes.

<bash-stdout></bash-stdout><bash-stderr>sudo: a terminal is required to read the password; either use the -S option to read from standard input or configure an askpass helper
sudo: a password is required
</bash-stderr>

The `!` prefix runs the command without a terminal, so sudo can't ask for the password there.

Please run this in a separate SSH terminal. The BFCL run is detached, so a second session doesn't affect it:

```bash
sudo dmidecode -t memory > ~/dmi-memory.txt
```

Then tell me, and I'll read `~/dmi-memory.txt` and fill in the memory type, speed, module sizes and channel count in "The PC" section. I'll also drop the "not read" note and the spec-only bandwidth estimate.

| | |
|---|---|

| Channels | **dual channel**: one module on channel A, one on channel B (both slots used; the board takes up to 128 GB) |
| Speed | rated DDR5-5600 (CL46), **running at 5200 MT/s** (the 8945HX's supported maximum) |
| Bandwidth | 5200 MT/s x 8 bytes x 2 channels = **83.2 GB/s** in theory; not measured yet (a test would have disturbed the BFCL run that was going) |

| Settings | swap 8 GiB file (3 MiB used); transparent huge pages `madvise`; no static huge pages |
| Page cache reads | the engine loads cached model files at 8.7-9.3 GiB/s (a single-threaded file read, not a bandwidth figure) |

Read with `sudo dmidecode -t memory` (saved as `~/dmi-memory.txt`).

'''
t = t[:s] + new + t[e:]
open(p, "w").write(t)
PYEOF

steps.reasoning_content: The differences I found look like typical model variation rather than errors—things like a path format change, added hashtags, or a written summary—pointing toward the template layer as the likely cause, though that's still unverified. I'm recording this finding in docs/3060M.md.

arguments.command:
cd /home/luwei/work/AI/Strata; python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p = "docs/3060M.md"; t = open(p).read()
anchor = "## Where the CPU time goes during BFCL"
assert anchor in t
new = '''### GSQ Coder, path A, thinking on: 400 items

The setup closest to Claude Code: native function calling, thinking on (`local-fc-think`, `max_tokens` 16384),
`multi_turn_base` + `multi_turn_miss_param`, 2026-10-03/04 (`~/work/AI/bfcl/runs/strata-gsq-A-on-...-think1`; run
detached with `setsid nohup` after 6 items, then `--resume`). Against the Halo's run of the same setup
(windows.md, `gsq-hip-A-on-...-gsq-think1`):

| GSQ Coder, path A, thinking on | overall (400) | base (200) | miss_param (200) | model time / entry | calls / entry | s / call | tok / call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp, Strix Halo | **60.2** | **79.0** | 41.5 | 97.5 s | 12.4 | 7.86 | 159 |
| Strata, RTX 3060 Laptop GPU | 52.5 [48,57] | 66.0 | 39.0 | **68.0 s** | 13.1 | **5.23** | 167 |

- **Context refusals: 11** (3 base, 8 miss_param), all "prompt + max tokens (16384) exceeds the context (32768)":
  prompts of 16.4K+ tokens with thinking's 16384-token budget do not fit in 32K. The Halo got 5 of these 11 right.
- **base is a real gap**: only llama.cpp right 35, only Strata right 9 (exact McNemar p < 0.001); 3 of the 35 are
  the refusals. miss_param is not: 25 and 20 (p = 0.55). Both together: 60 and 29 (p = 0.0013).
- Strata's extra base failures are wrong final states (instance_state_mismatch 53 vs 29). The items read like
  different choices by the model, not malformed calls: `cd "/temp"` where the Halo wrote `cd "temp"`, hashtags
  written into a tweet's text, a summary written into a file that should stay empty.
- Speed: 30% less model time per entry and 33% less per call, with about the same calls and output tokens
  (engine and hardware together). The whole run: 507 min of generation here, about 10.8 h on the Halo.

What differs from path B, where the engines score the same: path A goes through each server's chat template and
tool-call parser. llama.cpp ran the froggeric v22.5 template (it merges system messages and renders
mid-conversation ones, and tells the model to write Qwen3-style JSON calls); Strata ran the model's own template
and its XML tool format. With thinking on, how each template carries earlier turns' reasoning also differs. That is
the first suspect for the base gap; not tested. A test: the same run with the v22.5 template in Strata's pack
(`tokenizer/chat_template.jinja`), if Strata's parser reads its JSON calls.

'''
t = t.replace(anchor, new + anchor, 1)
open(p, "w").write(t)
PYEOF
grep -n "^### GSQ Coder, path A, thinking on" docs/3060M.md

steps.message:
The run has finished: 400 items in 8.5 hours of generation, scored, and the server is stopped. This time Strata scored lower than llama.cpp.

**GSQ Coder, path A, thinking on:**

| | Overall | base | miss_param | Model time per item | Time per call | Tokens per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp, Strix Halo | **60.2** | **79.0** | 41.5 | 97.5 s | 7.89 s | 159 |
| Strata, this PC | 52.5 | 66.0 | 39.0 | **68.0 s** | **5.21 s** | 166 |

- **11 context refusals.** These prompts were 16.4K+ tokens, and with thinking's 16,384-token answer budget they don't fit in 32K. The Halo got 5 of those 11 right, so the refusals cost about 1.25 points.
- **base: a real gap.** Item by item, llama.cpp alone got 35 right and Strata alone got 9 (McNemar p < 0.001). Only 3 of the 35 are refusals.
- **miss_param: no real difference** (25 against 20, p = 0.55).
- **What the failures look like:** most of Strata's extra base failures end in a wrong final state, but the calls themselves are well-formed. They read like different choices by the model: `cd "/temp"` where llama.cpp wrote `cd "temp"`, hashtags added to a tweet's text, a summary written into a file that should stay empty.
- **Speed:** 30% less model time per item, with about the same number of calls and output tokens.

**Likely cause, untested.** On path B (same prompt), the two engines scored the same. Path A adds each server's own chat template and tool parser:
- llama.cpp ran the froggeric v22.5 template, which handles mid-conversation system messages and tells the model to write JSON tool calls.
- Strata ran the model's own template with XML tool calls.
- With thinking on, the two templates also carry earlier turns' reasoning differently.

So the template is the main suspect, but I haven't verified it.

I added a section with these results, the error breakdown and the suspected cause to `docs/3060M.md`.

**Possible next steps:**
1. **Test the template:** run the same 400 items with the v22.5 template in Strata's pack (about 8.5 h). I'd first need to check that Strata's tool parser reads the JSON-style calls v22.5 asks for; I can do that in a few minutes before committing to a run.
2. **Remove the refusals:** run at 64K context. That would also cost some speed, because less VRAM is left for experts.

Should I check whether Strata's parser can handle the v22.5 template?

Two things in parallel. The 64K run is the long one, so I'll set it up first and start it detached. The parser check needs no GPU, so I can do it while that runs.

For 64K, I'll follow what setup does for this PC: `--max-context 65536` plus KV streaming (`--kv-resident 32768`). The whole KV cache lives in RAM (about 0.9 GB), and VRAM keeps only a 32K window, so the GPU should keep its share of experts. Checking the engine's options:

import json, sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from serve.frontend import ChatTemplate, OutputParser, openai_to_messages
tools = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "cd", "description": "Change directory.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"folder": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["folder"]}}},
         {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "ls", "description": "List files.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "boolean"}}}}}]

     "tool_calls": [{"id": "c1", "type": "function", "function": {"name": "cd", "arguments": "{\"folder\": \"temp\"}"}}]},

    {"role": "system", "content": "Note: hidden files matter."},          # mid-conversation system message
    {"role": "user", "content": "Now list with hidden files."}]}
messages, tls, kw = openai_to_messages(req)
out = {}
for name, path in (("strata default (pack)", "../Strata-data/packs/coder-iq1_m/tokenizer/chat_template.jinja"),
                   ("froggeric v22.4 (Halo)", sys.argv[1])):
    try:
        out[name] = ChatTemplate(path).render(messages, tools=tls, **kw)

reply = "Listing now.\n</think>\n\n<tool_call>\n<function=ls>\n<parameter=a>\ntrue\n</parameter>\n</function>\n</tool_call>"
ps = OutputParser(thinking=True, tools=tls); evs = ps.feed(reply) + ps.finish()
print("parser on an XML reply:", [(e.kind, e.call.name, e.call.arguments) for e in evs if e.kind == "tool_call"])

**CPU memory bandwidth, measured** (2026-10-04, machine idle). A STREAM-style test in C with OpenMP
(`benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`: `gcc -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fopenmp`, AVX-512 code): three 2 GiB
arrays (far larger than the 64 MiB L3), best of 5 passes, threads pinned with `OMP_PLACES`/`OMP_PROC_BIND=close`.
Bytes are counted as STREAM counts them (what the code loads and stores):

| threads (cores) | read | write | copy | triad | memset (NT stores) | memcpy (NT stores) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (core 1) | 46.2 | 24.9 | 31.4 | 35.8 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 2 (cores 1-2) | 51.4 | 24.8 | 34.1 | 37.9 | 65.4 | 46.4 |
| 4 (cores 1-4) | 50.9 | 24.1 | 32.4 | 36.6 | 59.1 | 48.5 |
| 8 (cores 1-8) | 52.0 | 24.2 | 31.5 | 35.5 | 57.0 | 49.1 |
| **15 (cores 1-15, Strata's workers)** | **54.6** | 24.1 | 30.9 | 34.6 | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 24.2 | 30.8 | 34.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with the SMT siblings) | 55.3 | 24.1 | 30.6 | 34.4 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, CCD1 only (cores 0-7) | 49.7 | 23.7 | 31.3 | 35.3 | 56.2 | 48.0 |
| 8, CCD2 only (cores 8-15) | 46.4 | 23.7 | 31.2 | 35.1 | 56.7 | 48.0 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 24.7 | 31.6 | 35.4 | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread rows came within 0.7 GB/s.

- **Read, what Strata's expert workers do** (they only read weights): about **55 GB/s** with 15-16 threads, 66% of
  the 83.2 GB/s theory; at most 57.0 with 4 threads on each chiplet. One thread already reaches 46 GB/s and 2-4
  reach 51: memory, not the number of cores, is the limit.
- **One chiplet** reads 46-50 GB/s, both together 55-57: each chiplet's Infinity Fabric link nearly fills the memory
  on its own, so spreading over both adds about 10%.
- **SMT siblings add nothing** (55.3 with 32 threads vs 55.5 with 16; memset drops from 54.5 to 49.3), which agrees
  with Strata leaving them idle.

steps.message:
Measured: this PC's CPU reads memory at **about 55 GB/s**, 66% of the 83.2 GB/s theoretical for dual-channel DDR5-5200. I added this to "The PC" in `docs/3060M.md`.

| Threads | Read | Write (non-temporal) | Copy (memcpy) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 46.2 | 62.3 | 36.2 |
| 15 (Strata's worker cores) | **54.6** | 55.2 | 48.2 |
| 16 (all cores) | 55.5 | 54.5 | 47.9 |
| 32 (with SMT) | 55.3 | 49.3 | 47.3 |
| 8, 4 on each chiplet | **57.0** | 56.1 | 50.0 |

GB/s; a repeat of the 15- and 16-thread runs came within 0.7 GB/s.

**What it means for Strata:**
- **Reads are the figure that matters.** The expert workers only read weights, so about 55 GB/s is the ceiling for computing experts on the CPU.
- **Memory is the limit, not cores.** One thread already reaches 46 GB/s, and 2–4 threads reach 51.
- **SMT adds nothing:** 55.3 with 32 threads against 55.5 with 16. That matches Strata leaving the SMT siblings idle, and the earlier conclusion that `--pool-workers 31` wouldn't help.
- **Both chiplets are needed for the full figure.** One chiplet alone reads 46–50 GB/s; both together reach 55–57.
- **Compared with the other links:** the experts the GPU doesn't hold are either computed by the CPU at up to about 55 GB/s, or copied to the GPU over PCIe at the measured 26.8 GB/s. The GPU's own memory is 336 GB/s (spec).

**How it was measured:**
- **The test:** a STREAM-style program in C with OpenMP, compiled with `-O3 -march=native -ffast-math` (so it uses AVX-512). It uses 2 GiB arrays, far larger than the cache, takes the best of 5 passes, and pins each thread to a core.
- **A pitfall caught along the way:** the first build without `-ffast-math` couldn't vectorize the read sum. It showed only 14 GB/s for one thread, which measured the adder rather than the memory.
- **Write numbers:** plain stores first read each cache line, so the "write" column counts only half the real traffic: 24 GB/s counted is about 48 GB/s actual. The table in the doc explains this.

The benchmark source is saved as `docs/benchmarks/2026-10-04-3060m-membw.c`, and the doc gives the build and run commands.

steps.reasoning_content: I'll run the test for each `--pcie-frac` value (0, 0.2, 0.55): starting a fresh server, warming up with a different prompt, then issuing the same measured prompt to record decode t/s, draft acceptance, and GPU expert-cache hit rate—verifying each run via absence of the probe line and the engine's process arguments.

arguments.command:
S=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-luwei-work-AI-Strata/fdd68fb3-d304-40df-b17b-5a7d3f2afd46/scratchpad; cat > $S/pcie_ab.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# decode with --pcie-frac X on the Coder: fresh server per value, one warm-up, then the measured request
S=$(dirname "$0"); cd /home/luwei/work/AI/Strata
python3 - > $S/pcie_prompt.json <<'PY'
import json
L = open("/mnt/evox2/large/work/AI/EngramHalo.cpp/src/llama-model-loader.cpp").read()
i = L.index("static std::vector<std::string> llama_get_list_splits"); j = L.index("\n}\n", i) + 3
p = "Rewrite this C++ function to be clearer and faster. Keep the behavior. Reply with the code.\n\n```cpp\n" + L[i:j] + "```"
json.dump({"model": "x", "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 512, "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False},
           "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": p}]}, open("/dev/stdout", "w"))
PY
for x in "$@"; do
  python3 -c "
import json; c = json.load(open('strata-coder-iq1_m.json')); c['args'] += ['--pcie-frac', '$x']
c['log'] = '$S/pcie-$x-engine.log'; json.dump(c, open('$S/pcie-$x.json', 'w'), indent=1)"
  python serve/server.py --engine strata --config $S/pcie-$x.json --port 8080 > $S/pcie-$x-server.log 2>&1 & pid=$!
  until grep -q "^ready: http" $S/pcie-$x-server.log; do kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null || { echo "server died ($x)"; tail -5 $S/pcie-$x-engine.log; exit 1; }; sleep 1; done
  args=$(ps -o args= -p $(pgrep -x strata) | grep -oE "\-\-pcie-frac [0-9.]+"); probe=$(grep -c "PCIe probe" $S/pcie-$x-engine.log)
  curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"x","temperature":0,"max_tokens":128,"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":false},"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Write a thread-safe LRU cache in C++."}]}' > /dev/null
  r=$(curl -s localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @$S/pcie_prompt.json)
  hit=$(grep -oE "expert cache [0-9.]+% hit" $S/pcie-$x-server.log | tail -1)
  echo "$r" | python3 -c "
import sys, json; r = json.load(sys.stdin); t = r['timings']; m = r['choices'][0]
print(f'pcie_frac $x (engine args: $args; probe lines: $probe): decode {t[\"predicted_per_second\"]} t/s over {t[\"predicted_n\"]} tokens, '
      f'drafts {t.get(\"draft_n_accepted\")}/{t.get(\"draft_n\")}, prefill {t[\"prompt_per_second\"]} t/s ({t[\"prompt_n\"]} tok), $hit, finish {m[\"finish_reason\"]}')
open('$S/pcie-$x-answer.txt', 'w').write(m['message']['content'] or '')"
  kill $pid; wait $pid 2>/dev/null; while pgrep -x strata >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
done
EOF
chmod +x $S/pcie_ab.sh; ps -eo pid,args | grep -E "engine/strata|run-bfcl" | grep -v grep; $S/pcie_ab.sh 0 0.2 0.55

steps.message:
Your prediction holds for decode: going from 0.55 down to 0.2 or 0 makes decode about **19% faster**. Between 0 and 0.2 there's no measurable difference.

**Coder IQ1_M, the same prompt, a fresh server for each value:**

| `--pcie-frac` | Decode | Tokens | Drafts accepted | GPU expert-cache hits | Prefill (274-token prompt) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **61.8 t/s** | 229 | 176/197 | 63.4% | 242.0 t/s |
| 0.2 | **61.3 t/s** | 229 | 176/197 | 66.3% | 241.5 t/s |
| 0.55 (this PC's current default) | 51.7 t/s | 230 | 176/186 | 76.2% | 238.6 t/s |

- **0 versus 0.2: the same.** Both produced byte-identical answers, so the 0.8% difference is noise.
- **0.55 is 16% slower** than 0.2. Its answer differs from byte 650 onwards, a sign that copied experts take a different numeric path, but its length and draft acceptance are as good or better, so the slowdown is real. Even though more expert lookups count as GPU hits (76% against 63–66%), decode gets slower: copying experts over PCIe costs more per token than computing them on the CPU from RAM.
- **This PC runs at 0.55 now.** The engine's probe measures 26.8 GB/s and keeps the 0.55 default, since anything at or above 20 GB/s does.

**Limits:**
- Each value was run once (n = 1). Only the 0.55 gap is clearly larger than run-to-run noise.

“The engine's probe measures 26.8 GB/s”跟你刚才测的CPU实际内存带宽差距大，对吗？做1，2测试

Yes, about a factor of two, and they're different links:
- **26.8 GB/s** is the engine's PCIe probe: host RAM to GPU over the PCIe 4.0 x16 link, about 85% of its roughly 31.5 GB/s theoretical maximum.
- **55 GB/s** is what the CPU cores read from RAM (66% of 83.2).

So per byte, computing a missing expert on the CPU has about twice the bandwidth of copying it to the GPU. Copying also reads that same RAM: the 26.8 GB/s of DMA comes out of the same ~55 GB/s the workers use. That's why a lower `--pcie-frac` decodes faster here.

Now tests 1 and 2, on both models, with a fresh server for each value:
- **Values:** Coder 0 / 0.2 / 0.55 / 0.75; UD-IQ4_XS 0 / 0.25 / 0.55 / 0.75.
- **Decode:** one warm-up, then the same prompt as before 3 times.
- **Prefill:** a 4K-token and a 16K-token prompt of real code (EngramHalo sources), 1 output token each, checked for no cache reuse.

Strata's own `tools/calibrate.py` notes that "the prompt path streams every expert whatever these settings say", so prefill may not respond to `--pcie-frac` at all. This test will show it.

def count(text):

    n = int(len(text) * tokens / count(text[:400000]) * len(text[:400000]) / len(text)) if False else int(tokens * 3.3)
    for _ in range(4):

        if abs(c - tokens) <= tokens * 0.01: break
        n = int(n * tokens / c)

    cfg = S / f"ab-{label}-{x}.json"; cfg.write_text(json.dumps(c))
    log = open(S / f"ab-{label}-{x}-server.log", "w")

    args = subprocess.run(["bash", "-c", "ps -o args= -p $(pgrep -x strata) | grep -oE -- '--pcie-frac [0-9.]+'"],

    for name, text in (("prefill 4K", texts[0]), ("prefill 16K", texts[1])):

        print(json.dumps({"model": label, "pcie_frac": x, "test": name, "tok_s": t["prompt_per_second"],

    p.terminate(); p.wait()
    while subprocess.run(["pgrep", "-x", "strata"], capture_output=True).returncode == 0: time.sleep(1)
